a price you do not control. Options give the right to buy at a strike set at grant and can be worth
zero. Different math (15.3.3–15.3.5). Ask for every grant: how many shares, what strike (if options),
vesting schedule, cliff, refresh policy, current fully diluted share count, and what happens to
unvested shares on termination — a question that changes value enormously and is routinely ambiguous.

**Sign-on and make-whole.** The most negotiable cash component because it comes from a different pool.
It exists to compensate foregone bonus, unvested equity, or a below-market salary you accepted — so **you
have a legitimate specific argument**: quantify the forfeiture. Non-competing bonus, lost equity value,
buyout of unvested RSUs are all citable. Check the clawback and negotiate it out or shorten it.

**Other components to inventory.** Relocation and temporary housing (how long, what standard, taxable?);
remote stipend and equipment; learning budget including conference travel; health plan tier and employer
contribution; retirement match and vesting; life and disability insurance; legal fees for contract
review (some companies pay — ask); immigration or visa fees; severance; unused PTO payout.

**The one-time vs recurring distinction.** The most valuable structural move is converting recurring comp
into one-time comp. A recurring increase permanently raises the band; a one-time payment is cheaper and
often easier to approve. If base is fixed, ask: "Is there flexibility in sign-on or a one-time equity
top-up?"

**Negotiation order of preference** — most to least valuable: (1) level/title, durable and it re-bases
everything; (2) equity grant size or refresh policy, compounding; (3) sign-on or one-time cash,
immediate and non-recurring; (4) base, durable but hardest; (5) scope, compounds most and is hardest;
(6) start date and flexibility, free and often unexploited; (7) benefits specifics.

**The document question.** Ask for the full written offer — equity terms, vesting, sign-on and clawback,
start date, title, level, contingencies. Verbal offers are not commitments and recruiting is high-volume.
If asked to wait for "something in writing later," ask for the terms summary now.

**Who can approve what.** Recruiters often have discretion up to a percentage on base and full discretion
on sign-on; above-band base needs the HM and sometimes a director or VP; equity refresh and level
require calibration. If the recruiter cannot move base, push them to take your case to whoever can — and
give them a written one-paragraph argument they can forward, which changes their incentive.

**Tax and jurisdiction.** Base and bonus are ordinary income; sign-on may be taxed as ordinary income
depending on structure; equity creates substantial tax events at vesting and sale; relocation packages
may be taxable. Your tax residency and the employer's country presence determine withholding and benefits
structure. Involve a tax professional before making an equity-heavy decision, not after.

### 15.3.3 Equity options: strike, vesting, cliff, dilution, and the maths

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**What an option is.** A right, not an obligation, to buy a fixed number of shares at a fixed strike
price for a fixed term, after which it expires worthless. Nothing to hold; tax on the spread at
exercise.

**Parameters and why each matters.** *Strike*: usually the fair market value at grant; a rising share
price creates positive spread. *Number of shares*: determine whether it is a share count or a percentage
of the company, and if a percentage, of what denominator — the single most consequential ambiguity in
early-stage equity. *Vesting*: usually four years monthly, sometimes with a one-year cliff, which defines
how much is at risk if you leave early. *Term*: typically ten years. *Post-termination exercise window*:
usually 90 days, which matters enormously if you leave. *Unvested treatment*: usually cancelled on
resignation; some companies offer single- or double-trigger acceleration, a significant benefit. *Early
exercise*: sometimes allowed, with a 12-month window and limited shares per period, which has tax
consequences and can finance a constrained candidate.

**The basic math.**
```
intrinsic value per share = max(0, current share price − strike)
total spread value        = intrinsic value per share × vested shares
```
Without the current share price you cannot value the grant. Ask for the most recent 409A valuation
price, or the current price from a recent financing. For comparison, RSUs settle automatically:
`value of vested RSUs = vested shares × share price` — simpler, and different in tax treatment.

**The dilution question candidates miss.**
```
your % after a primary round = your shares / (pre-money FD shares + new shares issued)
```
The critical fact is that option pools refresh. Much of a pool is reserved for future hires, so your
percentage falls from the next 50 engineers even with no new round. You need: fully diluted shares at
the last close; total pool authorized; shares already granted; the size of an upcoming financing and
how much is primary (dilutes you) versus secondary (does not); and how much pool is left.

**Worked dilution.** You hold 100,000 options; FD is 12,000,000; a new primary round issues 3,000,000.
Post-round FD is 15,000,000 and your percentage moves from ~0.83% to ~0.67% — a 20% relative
reduction, before the pool refresh, which can be comparable or larger.

**Scenario analysis.** Model at minimum a downside (failure or sub-round acquisition — often zero), a
base (modest growth, near or somewhat above the last round), and an upside, assigning your own
probabilities. Then compute expected value and compare it against the *non-equity delta* between offers.
If a lower-base offer at a mature company beats your expected value from early-stage equity, the
rational choice may be the boring offer. This is the most useful thing you will do in an early-stage
negotiation and almost nobody does it.

**Questions to ask, verbatim.** Current share price or latest 409A price? How many shares, and is that
a fixed number or a percentage — of what denominator? What is the strike, and is it evergreen or set
once at grant? Vesting schedule and is there a cliff? Post-termination exercise window, and what happens
to unvested shares on each termination type? Current fully diluted count and remaining pool?
Acceleration on change of control or termination? Refresh policy at your level, and has it historically
been at or below this grant? Is early exercise available and on what terms? What is the tax treatment,
and can I sell shares after I leave given transfer restrictions?

**Post-termination constraints.** Private companies restrict transfers, require approval for secondary
sales, and give existing holders a right of first refusal. A large paper position may be unsellable for
years. Price that illiquidity at a substantial discount when comparing to liquid public-company equity.

**The common mistake.** Accepting an early-stage offer because the headline is large. The headline is
shares, not value. Value requires a share price, a share count, a probability of that price, and a time
discount. Without all four you have no information.

### 15.3.4 RSUs: vesting schedule, refresh grants, and taxes

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**What an RSU is.** A promise to deliver shares on a schedule with tax withholding applied at
settlement. No strike, no exercise cost, no option expiry. Simpler than options and, for most
candidates, strictly better.

**Parameters.** *Grant size in shares*: set by level band, adjusted for performance and sometimes
negotiation. *Vesting*: commonly four years monthly, sometimes three or five, occasionally annual; RSUs
usually have no cliff, which is part of why they are preferred. *Termination treatment* — the critical,
policy-governed term: voluntary resignation before a vesting date typically forfeits unvested units;
involuntary termination without cause often vests a portion or accelerates, sometimes subject to tenure;
termination for cause vests nothing; on change of control, single-trigger acceleration is rare and
excellent while double-trigger (vest on termination after the change) is the common, better arrangement.
Ask for the actual policy in writing.

**The refresh grant — the most under-negotiated component.** Ongoing wealth comes from the annual refresh,
not the initial grant. Ask: what is the refresh policy by level and is there a published range? Does it
*maintain* my total unvested equity at a target multiple of my grant (structure), or is it a fixed
amount that shrinks as a share of my position (additive)? Does performance rating change it, and how
much? Do promotions produce an off-cycle refresh? Does the refresh vest on the same four-year monthly
schedule? This matters enormously over a multi-year tenure and almost never appears in negotiation: a
candidate who accepts a larger initial grant but a weaker refresh structure is worse off over five years.

**Tax mechanics.** At vesting, RSUs are taxed as ordinary income on the fair market value delivered,
withholding applied automatically, and the tax is owed on vesting *whether or not you sell*. This is the
phantom-income problem: a big bill with no cash from the sale. The fix is **sell-to-cover**: instruct
your broker to sell enough shares at vesting to cover withholding, keeping net shares and effectively
deferring tax to when you sell. Confirm the plan supports it and set it up *in advance*. At sale,
capital gains tax applies, at rates depending on your country and holding period; state and local tax can
change the outcome materially, and some locations tax vesting differently from gains. Non-US candidates may
be handled through structures with different consequences — involve a professional before your first large
vest.

**Modeling take-home.**
```
annual net shares = (grant / vesting years) × (1 − t)      t = effective withholding at vest
annual net value  = annual net shares × share price
```
Year one only; the position compounds as refreshes stack.

**Planning the vest event.** Confirm sell-to-cover with your broker; have a tax professional estimate the
bill; ensure liquid cash for the gap between withholding and the shares you want to keep, or you will be
forced to sell the whole grant. Check whether your vesting anniversary creates overlapping large events,
and whether any insider trading window restricts selling right after a vest.

**Negotiating RSUs.** Initial grant size is banded by level, so an above-band request needs a story: a
competing offer, a level argument, a strong signal. Equity is harder to move than base but often easier
than people expect, particularly at companies with visible share prices and a strong market. Equity
refresh and promotion policies are the higher-leverage long-term ask. If comparing two offers with
different equity *types*, do not compare counts — see 15.3.6. Ask-on-top-hire grants, promotion-
triggered off-cycle refreshes, acceleration provisions, and same-day sell-to-cover are all worth raising as
diligence questions; companies will explain standard policies even when they will not change them.

**The uncomfortable truth.** RSUs are a bet on one company's stock, a bet on your continued employment,
and a bet on your level not stagnating. A large refresh-based package at a company you believe in often
beats a smaller one at a company you are unsure of, because the continuity assumption dominates.

### 15.3.5 Startup equity risk: 409A, liquidation preferences, and dilution math

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Five questions before you value early-stage equity.** (1) What is the actual current share price, per
the latest 409A valuation or financing? (2) What is the fully diluted share count, including the entire
pool? (3) What are the liquidation preferences, and how much of the company is taken off the top before
common participates? (4) What is the expected time to liquidity, and is acquisition plausible at all?
(5) How dilutive is the plan, and how much pool remains? Without all five, any valuation you compute is
fiction.

**409A valuations.** Under US rules, employee shares are typically priced at an independent appraised fair
market value, refreshed at least annually and often only on a triggering event. Practically: it is a
low-water mark used for tax, not a forecast, and often not a signal about the company's actual view. It can
lag badly — long after a round at a higher price, the 409A may sit well below it. Ask for the latest 409A
price *and date* separately from the latest round price *and date*. A low 409A is **not** cheap shares:
with the same share count it gives you the same percentage of a more valuable company; it only lowers your
tax basis today. After an up round a company usually triggers a refresh; if it has not, ask why and when.

**Dilution math.**
```
your post-money % = your shares / FD shares post-round
future FD shares  = current FD + unallocated pool + new primary shares in future rounds
your future %     = your shares / future FD
```
The *unallocated pool* term is the one candidates forget. A plan often authorizes enough pool to cover
years of hiring, so a meaningful fraction is reserved for people who are not you. Ask: total pool,
granted to date, unallocated balance. Then assume the unallocated portion gets granted. Worked: you hold
100,000 of 12,000,000 FD = 1.50%; pool authorized 2,000,000, granted 900,000, unallocated 1,100,000; a
further primary round of 3,000,000 gives `future FD = 16,100,000` and `your future % = 0.62%` — a **59%
relative reduction** before any bad outcome.

**Liquidation preferences.** A 1× non-participating preference means preferred investors get their
investment back before common shareholders see anything. With a pool and preferences ahead of you, the
break-even acquisition price can sit far above the last round price.

**Worked preference waterfall.** Assume 10,000,000 FD shares; 4,000,000 preferred at 1×
non-participating, $1.50/share; 6,000,000 common and option shares including your 200,000. Acquired for
$30,000,000, which implies ~$3.00/share if split evenly.
```
1. Preference first: 4,000,000 × 1.50                =  6,000,000
2. Remaining to common + options: 30,000,000 − 6,000,000 = 24,000,000
3. Preferred total per share: 1.50 + (24,000,000 / 10,000,000 = 2.40) = 3.90
4. Common and options receive 2.40 per share
5. Your 200,000 shares = 480,000, against a headline of 3.00 — a 20% haircut
   from the naive number, purely because of preferences.
```
Your per-share value is not the company's per-share value unless preferences are nil or small relative to
the exit value.

**Scenario framing.** Model at least: failure (zero); acquisition below the last round (often near zero
after preferences); acquisition near the last round; and a meaningful up-round outcome. Assign your own
honest probabilities. Two structural facts should anchor your pessimism: most venture-backed companies
never reach a liquidity event, and among those that do, many exit below the last round price. Use your own
judgment about the specific company — I am not going to hand you a statistic I cannot verify.

**A low 409A as an advantage.** When you early-exercise or RSUs vest, taxable income is based on the 409A,
so a low price means a smaller immediate tax bill. If the 409A later refreshes upward, tax on the gain
becomes payable on exercise or sale — deferred, not eliminated. Ask a tax advisor about early-exercise
financing and about a low 409A followed by a later refresh creating a large deferred tax liability.

**Startup-specific questions.** Last round's price per share, size, primary or secondary? Total pool and
unallocated balance? Preferred terms — multiple, participating or not, seniority across series? 409A price
and date? Run rate, headcount, and burn? Plan for the next raise and how much primary will it issue?
Repurchase rights, drag-along, or ROFR affecting you? Is there single-trigger acceleration, and on what
change of control?

**Get a professional.** Bring an equity specialist to the offer stage if the equity is material; startup
compensation is a specialist domain and the cost is trivial relative to the amount at stake. If the
company will not pay, use a discounted-fee professional.

**The honest conclusion.** Early-stage equity is an option, not a valuation. Compare offers on what you
can price with certainty — base, cash bonus, sign-on, benefits — and treat early-stage equity as a bonus
that may be worth zero. A company requiring low cash compensation *because* of the equity story is a
warning sign, not a perk.

### 15.3.6 Total compensation comparison: how to normalize offers

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Why normalization is the highest-value activity in offer evaluation.** Offers arrive in incomparable
units — base, total cash, "total compensation" including an unvalued equity grant, a startup's post-money
share count. Comparing them unnormalized compares different currencies and reliably produces the wrong
decision.

**The framework.** One row per offer, with columns for: base; target bonus %; sign-on and other cash;
equity type (RSUs / options / none); equity units; assumed share price; strike; vesting schedule; refresh
policy; present-value factor; probability of outcome; probability you remain employed; benefits value;
retirement value; leave value.

**Step 1 — present value of cash.**
```
PV cash = base × years + bonus_target × base × years × realism + (sign-on + other cash)
```
Apply a cost-of-living adjustment if geographies differ materially, and be explicit about whose cost of
living you are normalizing to — yours, not the employer's.

**Step 2 — equity per unit type.**
```
RSUs:    value per unit = share price
Options: value per unit = max(0, price − strike) × P(price > strike at expiry)
```
For long-dated employee options, Black–Scholes is more precise; a practical approximation takes intrinsic
value times a conservative probability factor. Private-company transfer restrictions warrant a further
illiquidity discount.

**Step 3 — discount for liquidity and time.**
```
PV equity = gross value × P(survives to your exit) × P(company outcome) × (1 − liquidity discount)
```
For RSUs at a mature public company many candidates use `grant × current price` and treat vesting as an
income stream — but then they must remember that annual vesting creates annual tax, which reduces net
accumulation each year.

**Step 4 — recurring non-cash components.**
```
annual benefits = employer health contribution + retirement match (to the extent you participate)
                + paid leave (days × (base + bonus) / working days) + items you will actually use
```
Exclude anything you will not use. A generous health plan you never use is worth its premium, not its
potential.

**Step 5 — multi-year view.** Compare over three years, not one: base growth, one promotion in year two
or three, and the refresh policy at each level dominate the year-one picture. Extend to five years for a
long-term home. Run a sensitivity table on the share-price assumption at ±30%, because for equity-heavy
offers that assumption dominates the result.

**Common normalization errors.** Comparing a startup's share count to a public RSU count. Forgetting that
unvested equity at a company with accelerating stock beats the same grant at a flat one. Ignoring annual
vest tax. Counting the employer retirement match as full comp when it requires your own salary deferral
to get it. Pricing "unlimited PTO" without an estimate of realistic utilization at that company.
Ignoring vesting forfeiture risk — if you might leave in 18 months, year-one value is roughly the vested
portion. Treating equity as available in year one when the schedule says otherwise.

**Model the non-monetary terms too**, because they compound: scope (what you will own in 18 months —
scope growth drives future raises); manager quality and stability (churn at 12 months is a large hidden
cost); team trajectory; on-call intensity; learning curve; location and commute; and reversibility
(signing clawbacks make exits harder).

**The decision output.** Three numbers: expected total value over three years, your confidence interval
around it, and the non-monetary factor you are willing to trade money for. Then choose and write down why
*before* negotiating, so the negotiation is about extracting the last 10–20% rather than discovering what
you want. A full worked example is in the worked-examples section; the governing habit is that no two
numbers are comparable until they are on the same date with the same units and assumptions.

### 15.3.7 The negotiation: sequencing and who goes first

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Sequence 1 — setting up (before the offer).** Level and role scope. These should be settled before
comp is discussed, because band and equity sizing follow from level. When a recruiter raises level, do
not immediately accept: ask what the scope is, what the team looks like, and what success looks like in
year one. Level changes made early are far cheaper than after an offer is issued.

**Sequence 2 — getting the first offer.** Never negotiate hard against one option. Aim for two or more
live processes, ideally reaching offer stage at similar times. This is the entire strategic reason
concurrency matters.

**Sequence 3 — anchoring.** With a competing offer or credible market anchor, **you go first and anchor
high**. With nothing else, let them go first and ask what the approved range is; their number becomes
your reference and anchoring against yourself is irreversible.

**Sequence 4 — the written offer.** Get title, level, base, bonus percentage, equity units and type,
vesting, strike if applicable, sign-on and its clawback, start date, and any contingencies in writing.
Negotiate from the document, not a verbal summary.

**Sequence 5 — the negotiation.** Present asks as a *package*, not a list. Explain the basis once,
clearly, in terms of scope and market, then list three or four asks. Keep the tone collaborative: you are
helping them solve a problem they also want solved.

**Sequence 6 — closing.** Confirm final terms in writing, ask the timeline to signature, ask what happens
between now and start, then decide.

**Who you negotiate with.** The *recruiter* is your first line: they have discretion, want to close, and
control the process — give them a written, forwardable argument. The *hiring manager* controls level and
team budget and often base, so a polite, specific conversation about scope and level is often more
effective than arguing base with a recruiter; ask the recruiter to facilitate it. *HR/HRBP* owns policy
and approval; the recruiter will brief them, so provide the case in a forwardable form. *Comp committee*
handles out-of-band equity; the recruiter advocates for you.

**Going first, precisely.** Two cases where anchoring high is right: you have a competing written offer
at or above their level, or you have strong specific market evidence for that level and scope. Even then,
anchor as a range with reasoning, and be prepared to defend it. An anchor you cannot defend is worse
than a modest one you can, because it burns credibility you need for the second ask.

**Letting them go first.** Right when you are unsure what is approved, when internal candidates are
invisible to you, or when your current package is below market and any number you name risks anchoring
under their expectation.

**Multi-ask structure, most to least likely to be approved.** One-time items (sign-on, relocation,
make-whole); level or title with a scope argument; equity amount or an off-cycle top-up; refresh policy
or promotion-triggered grants; base; everything else. Anchor on one component, concede on another.
Conceding nothing signals you are not collaborating; conceding the important one signals you are.

**Time as a lever.** Genuine flexibility is worth real money: "I could start earlier if it helps close
this out," "I have two weeks of notice." Offer them where true.

**The written one-paragraph case.**
```
Role:        <title/level> at <company>, <scope in one sentence>
Market:      <two specific observations — comparable roles, levels, packages — with dates>
Equity:      <what you have, or that you do not>
Request:     <the specific asks, ranked>
Flexibility: <start date, location, anything genuinely open to trade>
```
Short enough to forward. This makes your recruiter an advocate rather than a messenger.

**Do not negotiate things you have not verified.** Ask directly: "Is a sign-on typical for this role
here?" That question is normal and it tells you what is available.

**Handling a hard no.** Ask what *is* movable and move the energy there. If everything is immovable you
have three options: accept, escalate with a level or scope argument, or accept and treat it as information
for the next process. Accepting gracefully has real option value; burning bridges has negative option value.

**One negotiation at a time.** Do not negotiate with Company A while waiting on Company B's decision, and
never disclose dual negotiations except where a genuine deadline exists. Confirm agreement in writing
after every round of changes, briefly — verbal-only negotiations produce expensive misunderstandings about
vesting and clawbacks.

### 15.3.8 Negotiation scripts for the actual conversations

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Opening frame — never name a number first.**
> "I'm glad we're at this stage. Before we talk about specifics, I'd like to make sure we're aligned
> on scope and level, because that's what everything else keys off. Can you walk me through how you
> see the role and where it's leveled?"

**Level conversation.**
> "Based on the scope — owning X end to end, with Y and Z teams as partners — my experience lines up
> with <level> rather than <level>. How does leveling work here, and who would I need to convince?
> Here's the work that supports it: <two concrete examples, one with a result>."

**When asked "what are you looking for?"**
> "Before I answer — can I ask how the band is structured for this level, and where my experience
> sits inside it? I'd rather optimize for the whole package and for the role being correctly leveled
> than negotiate one line item."

**If you must give a number.**
> "For base, I'm targeting the top of what's approved for this level given the scope, and I have
> flexibility on structure. For total cash with the target bonus, that puts me around <range>. And
> I'd expect the equity grant to be sized for the level we settle on."

**Naming a competing offer.**
> "I have a written offer at <level> with <structure>, and I want to be straightforward that it's
> active. The scope here is what I care most about and the total package is comparable. If you can
> move on the areas below, I'd have difficulty saying no."

Truth only. "Active" means the deadline is real. Never fabricate a competing offer — the details are
easy to verify and the consequence is permanent.

**The ask, as a package.**
> "Here's what would let me say yes quickly. First, base at <X>, top of the band for the scope.
> Second, the initial grant at <N> shares, sized to the level. Third, a signing bonus of <amount>
> covering what I forfeit leaving now. Fourth, an off-cycle review at <month> tied to scope. If base
> is fixed, I'm open to moving the one-time components instead."

**Signing bonus justification.**
> "The amount is the one-time forfeiture: my target bonus pro-rated for the year plus the unvested
> equity I can't take with me, which comes to <amount>. If cash isn't workable, an equivalent
> one-time equity grant is fine. Can you check with <approver>? I can put the argument in writing."

**Base justification that is not about your needs.**
> "My current base is <X>, but I don't want to anchor there, so let me give you the market picture:
> for this scope and level in <market> I'm seeing <range> based on <specific sources>. I'm asking for
> the top of that because of the <specific depth> work — the <thing> migration and the <thing>
> reliability work are directly relevant to what this team is solving."

**When base cannot move.**
> "I understand base is fixed at this level. Would the company be open to a one-time equity top-up,
> or a signing bonus to make me whole on the forfeiture? Those are the two that would bridge the gap."

**When they ask what would make you say yes.**
> "If you can get me to <X> on base, or equivalent on the package, I'm in. I'm not going to hold out
> for something I don't think exists — I want to work here."

**Response to "we don't have room."**
> "Understood. What *is* flexible? If it's helpful, here's what I could work with: <specific trade>
> for <specific trade>. I have flexibility on <X>."

**Post-offer, still deciding.**
> "I want to be thoughtful, and honest: I have another process at a similar level with a decision
> point on <date>. I'm evaluating you very seriously — could you get me the final terms by <date>?"

**Declining with grace.**
> "I've decided to go with <other company>. I want you to hear it from me first because you've been
> straightforward. Thank you for <specific thing>. If your search ever needs a <your skill>, call me."

**Escalating to the hiring manager.**
> "I'd like to talk through two things, both about the role rather than money: how the scope is
> leveled, and where the team expects this hire to go in the first year. Does the number change if
> the scope is what I described?"

**Ask about titles carefully.** Titles vary by convention and cost nothing, so companies grant them more
freely than money — but some promotions trigger comp review, some titles are reserved, and a "principal"
title implying the wrong level creates administrative problems. Ask whether the title is level-mapped.

**Silence is a tool.** After you make your case, stop talking. The other side frequently fills the gap
with something you did not expect.

### 15.3.9 Counter offers and why they often fail

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**What a counter offer is.** Your current employer matching part or all of a new offer to keep you.
Common, and less useful than candidates hope.

**Why it usually fails.** (1) You have already decided — counters work when genuinely undecided, and once
you have accepted elsewhere your commitment is visible and trust is broken. (2) The money treats the
symptom — the reason you wanted to leave is rarely salary, and a counter that does not address the
underlying problem postpones the exit. (3) The match is incomplete — frequently base but not equity, or
this year but not next, discovered after you have resigned. (4) Trust is damaged — many managers see
an offer-accepting-then-returning employee as a flight risk, and some deals become "we promoted you but
we will be reviewing you carefully." (5) It is a bridge with a cost — you will likely leave again from a
weaker position having burned goodwill, and the second search is harder. (6) Internal equity breaks —
being raised to a level others see you as may expose you in the next reorganization. (7) Timing —
counters arrive late, compressing your decision window, and the raise often lands in a closed budget cycle.

**Where counter offers are best.** When you have not yet decided and the current job is genuinely
attractive; when the gap is small and specific and you can articulate what the raise would fix; when the
offer being countered is lateral with no growth; and when the real problem was one specific fixable
thing — a bad project, a missing mentor, a stalled promotion — and the company addresses *that*.

**Evaluate a counter offer seriously.** Is it permanent or a one-time retention payment that expires if
you leave within a window — a bribe with a timer? Does it change title and level, or only the number? Is
it accompanied by real scope change? Is it paid from a budget that could be clawed back or contingent on a
rating? What happens if you decline, and who knows you negotiated? Does it come with an implied longer
tenure?

**The conversation.** Be direct, brief, and honest.
> "I want to be straightforward: I've been offered <X> and have until <date> to decide. I've thought
> seriously about staying, because I like <specific thing>. But <specific problem> is what led me to
> look, and a number alone doesn't change that. I'm open to talking about what would change it — but
> I want to be honest that I can't commit without that."

**If you take a counter.** Leave in writing with a respectful notice, thank them, and stay committed for
at least six months if you can. Then plan the real exit with the same discipline. If the counter resolved
nothing structural, you are in a worse market position than when you started, having re-established
loyalty you did not feel.

**The ethical dimension.** Accepting a counter after accepting another offer is a legitimate business
decision but breaks a commitment to someone who made you an offer. Do it only when genuinely torn and the
counter addresses a real reason for leaving. Tell the other company promptly and courteously either way.

**Prevention.** If a counter is likely, keep the search quiet, do not discuss your intentions broadly, and
do not let enthusiasm for leaving leak. But do not lie if asked directly — that ends the relationship
permanently. **The generalization:** counter offers are a symptom of a weak internal alternative. Build
one — a promotion case, a role change, a transfer, a manager conversation with a deadline.

### 15.3.10 Multiple offers: real deadlines and real leverage

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**The goal of parallel processes.** Two or more live late-stage processes reaching decision points at
similar times give you information about your market value, genuine leverage, and the ability to choose
on substance rather than anxiety.

**Never fabricate a competing offer or a deadline.** This is the one hard rule of offer negotiation.
Fabricated deadlines are detectable — recruiters talk, companies call each other, dates do not survive
one verification call. The cost when caught is not a lost negotiation but a permanent reputation cost in
a market smaller than you think.

**Real deadlines are legitimate and common.** Written offer letters with a decision date; cohort or batch
interview schedules ending on a specific date; fiscal or budget deadlines ("offers must be extended by
the 15th to make this quarter"); a competing process's actual written deadline; start-date constraints
from notice. Use them when they exist, and attach the fact rather than the claim.

**Creating a real deadline when there isn't one.** Ask each recruiter: "How long should I take to
decide? Are there dates I should be aware of?" and take the time they give you. Slow-walk the second
process slightly so both offers converge, honestly. Ask for an extension in writing — companies grant
these routinely and the request signals seriousness. Or anchor your timeline in something real.

**Staging two offers well.** Inform each recruiter truthfully that you have another process and a
decision point. Ask each for a short extension citing that point. Use one as a reference point for the
other without violating either process's confidentiality terms — stating "I have a competing offer at
<similar level> and <similar total>" is generally acceptable; forwarding the other company's letter
without permission usually is not. Negotiate to a fair package at both, then compare on normalized numbers.

**Extending a deadline gracefully.**
> "I have a decision point on <date> from another process that I need to honor. I'm close to a
> decision here. Is there flexibility on the response date? If it helps, I can give you my answer in
> writing within a few hours of <date> so your team can use the time."

The last clause converts a delay for the company into a small cost for you.

**When two offers are close.** Do not turn them into a public bidding war. Work each to a fair package,
compare on normalized value and non-monetary terms, and accept the better one. Within roughly 5% on
normalized total, non-monetary factors should decide, not the last few thousand dollars — the switching
cost of a poor role far exceeds 5% of one year's pay. For very different kinds of offer (mature RSUs
versus startup options, staff scope versus senior stability) use the multi-year model (15.3.6) with
explicit assumptions, especially about equity, then decide which risk you are willing to hold.

**"I need to think about it" management.** Give a real deadline, not an open-ended one: companies fill
open windows with other candidates. A candidate who commits to a time and delivers is remembered well. If
you need more, ask explicitly with a reason and a new date.

**Do not accept verbally and keep negotiating.** Once you accept, leverage is gone and the relationship is
damaged. Get the terms you want in writing first.

**The offer that is too good to be true.** If a package sits far outside the band you researched after
two conversations, ask directly: "Is there something unusual about this role or the budget I should
know about?" Sometimes the answer is a competing internal candidate, an approved exception, or a reorg.
Sometimes it reveals the offer is for a different scope than you assumed.

**Keep the other company informed.** When you pass, tell them promptly and specifically. When you accept,
tell the loser first if you can — it costs nothing and preserves the market.

### 15.3.11 Benefits evaluation: health, retirement, leave, and equity-adjacent value

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Why this deserves attention.** Benefits can be worth five to fifteen percent of total compensation,
they are often negotiable in aggregate when the company wants you, and the highest-value items are not in
the offer letter.

**Health insurance — evaluate the plan, not the contribution.** What matters: employer contribution
amount and whether it is a flat subsidy or a percentage of premium; plan type (HMO, PPO, HDHP, EPO) and
network breadth where you actually live; deductible, out-of-pocket maximum, and coinsurance — the numbers
that determine what a serious illness costs you; family coverage cost and whether dependent premiums are
subsidized; prescription, mental health, fertility and family-forming coverage, which vary enormously and
are a real quality-of-life difference; and HSA eligibility — a high-deductible plan with an HSA
contribution is excellent for a healthy person and terrible for a chronic-condition household, which is a
genuine calculation, not a preference. Also check network adequacy where you live and whether your
doctors are in-network; surprise bills and out-of-network denials are a real financial risk. Method: get
the plan's summary of benefits and coverage, compute your expected annual cost plus your worst case, and
compare those numbers across offers in money, not by plan name.

**Retirement.** Match formula (percentage of your deferral, percentage of salary, cap on the match, cap
on eligible deferral), vesting on employer contributions, contribution limits, plan investment options (a
decent low-cost index lineup is a real benefit), and any discretionary contribution. The one-line
calculation: a 50% match up to 6% of salary means your employer adds 3% of salary; compounded over five
years that is real money — and a two-year cliff is worth knowing about.

**Leave.** Price it honestly. Annual leave: days granted × your daily rate. Public holidays observed in
your country, and how many the company actually gives. Sick leave — paid, unpaid, capped or unlimited-
and-untracked. Parental leave: weeks, all parents or primary only, fully paid, and whether tenure and
equity continue during it. Bereavement. Sabbatical policy if one exists — sabbaticals at senior levels are
real, quantifiable value worth asking about explicitly.

**Equity-adjacent value that is easy to miss.** Refresh grants (recurring value absent from a one-year
comparison, 15.3.4); off-cycle promotion grants; education and conference budgets including travel;
certification or exam cost coverage; equipment budgets and whether you choose the hardware; home-office
setup and whether it survives termination; commuter benefits. Then on-call compensation, relocation detail
(below), legal fees for contract review, immigration or visa support including dependents, severance terms,
and unused PTO payout.

**Work-model benefits.** Remote stipend and equipment, coworking allowance, travel frequency and
expectations, and — most important — how the written policy is enforced in practice. Ask current
employees; the written policy and the practice diverge nearly everywhere.

**How to negotiate benefits.** Rarely item by item. What works: "Is there flexibility in the sign-on to
offset what I'm losing on healthcare?" — the company cares far less about which form compensation takes than
you do. Ask for a one-time payment to bridge a coverage gap when changing plans. In a competitive market,
candidates who ask precise informed questions about benefits get taken more seriously; specificity is
itself a signal. Where a benefit is a real hardship — family coverage cost, a needed medical device, a
school-age child's needs — a case-specific accommodation is often possible, and HR is generally more
flexible than candidates assume.

**Who to ask.** The recruiter for plan documents and official written policies; benefits teams directly for
plan specifics (they will answer, and asking signals you read the paperwork); and your *future colleagues*
for reality. Both are necessary, and only the second predicts your experience. **The summary:** convert
every benefit you will actually use into annual dollars for the spreadsheet; treat the rest as zero.

### 15.3.12 Contracts, non-competes, IP assignment, and what to flag

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Read before you sign.** The moment of signature is when your leverage is lowest. Read the employment
agreement, IP assignment, confidentiality agreement, any non-compete, and the equity plan documents
*before* accepting, and ask questions while you still have alternatives.

**Non-competes.** A restriction on working in the same industry, at the same companies, or in the same
role, for a period after you leave, often with compensation attached. Enforceability varies sharply by
jurisdiction: void or unenforceable in some places, strictly enforced and well-paid in others. Do not
assume — have a lawyer in the relevant jurisdiction tell you, or at minimum check the statutory position
for where you will live and where the company is incorporated.

**What to look for.** *Scope*: all industries, all companies above a size, or a named competitor list? A
clause barring any software work in a broad field is materially different from one naming competitors.
*Duration*: six months is very different from two years. *Geography*: nationwide is very different from one
metro area. *Compensation during the restriction*: paid restrictions are often enforceable and sometimes
valuable; unpaid ones are what get litigated. *Interaction with at-will*. *Choice of law and venue*, which
may not be your state. *Garden leave*: paid non-solicitation or non-dealing periods, sometimes at a
fraction of salary.

**Practical response.** Ask before accepting, neutrally: "I'd like to review the IP assignment and any
restrictive covenants — could you send them in advance so I'm not rushed?" Completely normal; a
reasonable recruiter will not blink. A company that requires you to sign something unreviewed at offer
stage is telling you how it will treat you later.

**Non-solicitation** is separate and common, usually narrower and more enforceable than a non-compete.
Understand it, because it constrains your next job's ability to recruit from them and may extend to
"employees" broadly — ask whether that means everyone at signing, everyone at termination, or your team.

**IP assignment.** Mostly reasonable by default. Check the *scope of "inventions"* — whether it covers
anything conceived during employment or everything touching the employer's business; a properly scoped
clause covers work product created with employer resources or relating to their business, while a clause
capturing independent work is a problem. Check for *prior-invention exclusions*: if there is no schedule
listing what you brought with you, ask to add one and attach a written list of your prior work. Note
*moral rights waivers* in some jurisdictions. Check *post-termination obligations* — how long, and
whether it purports to reach general skills and knowledge, which no agreement can legitimately extinguish.
And check how it *interacts with open source and side projects*: whether outside work is permitted and
whether anything is restricted.

**Confidentiality.** Understand the survival period, whether it purports to cover information you knew from
a *previous* employer — it cannot reasonably require you to keep your old employer's secrets from your new
one, though this arises in practice and is a real ethical situation — and whether anything is carved out
for general knowledge and skills. Include the right to discuss your work in general, non-confidential
terms, because a clause prohibiting even that is genuinely awkward in interviews.

**Equity plan documents.** Read the grant agreement, the plan, exercise and sale restrictions, the
post-termination exercise window, good/bad leaver provisions, and change-of-control treatment. Confirm your
grant is or will be reflected in a board-approved plan and that you will receive a copy. Confirm treatment
on termination for cause versus without cause.

**Other clauses to check.** At-will versus fixed term; offer contingencies that would void the offer
(background check, references, immigration status, signing-bonus clawback) and that you understand; the
notice period and whether resigning forfeits the signing bonus — almost always it does, so confirm the
clawback period and exceptions; bonus plan terms (discretionary or written criteria, and whether
clawback applies after payment); relocation repayment provisions; arbitration clauses and class-action
waivers, which mean giving up a jury and class actions; governing law and venue; death and disability
provisions for equity; and change-of-control treatment of unvested equity.

**What to flag to a lawyer.** Everything above if the package is material, plus any non-compete, unusual
IP language, anything unusual for your jurisdiction, anything you do not understand, and any change made to
a document after your first review. One hour with a lawyer in your jurisdiction is cheap insurance on a
package worth six figures a year.

**Questions to ask the recruiter.** "Could you send the employment agreement, IP assignment, and any
restrictive covenants in advance?" "Are there contingencies attached to the offer?" "Is there a clawback
on the signing bonus, and over what period?" "Will I get the equity plan documents before I sign?" "Is
there anything specific to this role or this jurisdiction?" None of these are unreasonable, and all are
better asked before you accept.

### 15.3.13 Relocation terms

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Know what "relocation" includes, because packages vary enormously.** Temporary housing (weeks or
months, what standard, taxable?); a lump sum or reimbursed expenses, and whether it is taxable;
house-hunting trips and who pays travel; household-goods shipment with coverage limits; loss-on-sale
coverage on your current home; commuter or interim living assistance if your household cannot move
immediately; family support — partner job search help, school placement, dependent visas; mortgage
assistance or buyout of a remaining lease; visits back to your origin city; and the eligibility timeline
plus what happens if you leave within 6, 12, or 24 months.

**The clawback is the term that matters most.** Most packages require staying for a period, typically one
year, sometimes two. Leaving early can trigger repayment of the full or a prorated amount. Ask for exact
written terms, and ask whether the clause survives if you are terminated, if the role changes, or if a
spouse's career is the reason you cannot follow. Getting the carve-outs in writing is worth real money,
because the most common reason to leave early is a family or health event you could not have predicted.

**Tax treatment.** Relocation benefits are generally taxable unless you meet a statutory exclusion for
employees meeting distance or time requirements in many jurisdictions. Ask whether the package is
grossed up — the company paying tax on your behalf — which is a material difference in net value. Compute
the after-tax amount; a taxable package is worth noticeably less than its face.

**House-hunting discipline.** Do not buy a house before your start date. New hires make expensive
decisions under interstate-move pressure. Rent for the first several months, visit neighborhoods in
person, and use the temporary housing period as the exploration window. This is the single most common
early mistake in relocation and very hard to undo.

**Cost it yourself, comprehensively.** Beyond the package: your housing-cost delta; moving costs; dual
housing; school or childcare changes; commute time in the new city; visits home for the family; and often
largest, the effect on a partner's career and social network. A package offsetting three months of dual
housing is not compensation for a trailing partner's career cost, even though many people treat it as if
it were.

**Remote-in-hybrid reality.** If the role is hybrid in the new city, verify before signing: how many
days, per-team or per-company, can it change after you start, and is the office where the work is or a
formality. Then check the office location. A "hybrid" role in a suburb with bad transit is a hidden
relocation failure.

**Questions to ask.** Total value of the package and which parts are taxable? Is there a gross-up? What
is the minimum stay and the clawback formula, and what are the carve-outs? What is temporary housing
like — where, how long, what size? Can I get a home-finding visit, and when should I arrive? What does
the team do about hybrid schedules in practice? What help exists for a partner's job search and dependent
visas?

**Negotiation points.** People routinely negotiate a longer temporary housing period, a non-clawed
portion, a larger lump sum, coverage for a partner's job search, or flexibility to start remotely for the
first month and relocate later. These are often easier to get than base money, because they come from a
different budget.

**When relocation is not worth it.** If the destination's cost of living is dramatically higher, the
package will not close the gap and the headline number is misleading. Do the arithmetic on net cash in
hand, not on the offer letter. And if a partner's career is sacrificed, decide explicitly whether that is
acceptable rather than discovering later.

### 15.3.14 Remote, hybrid, and visa considerations

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**The work model as compensation.** Remote, hybrid, and onsite are different jobs with different totals.
Adjust: commute time has a real annual cost in hours, and those hours are not recoverable. A fully remote
offer in a lower-cost city can net more than a higher base onsite elsewhere. Model after-tax and
after-commute.

**Questions to settle before signing.** Required office days per week, and whether it is a company policy,
team policy, or one manager's preference — get the answer from two people, because these diverge. Who
chooses which days, and are core days imposed. What "remote" means geographically: same time zone, same
country, anywhere; same country usually implies local employment terms, which is safer for you.
Compensation by location, whether the offer is location-specific, and what happens if you later move.
Time-zone overlap hours and whether meetings are distributed or concentrated. Travel frequency and who
pays. Equipment and connectivity budgets and whether they survive termination. And what happens to your
role if the policy changes later — realistically they can change it, so know how much notice you would get.

**Red flags in remote arrangements.** "Remote" with more on-site days than the local team gets; a policy
changeable at any time without notice; location-specific pay that would cut substantially if you relocate;
no written statement of your employment country and governing law; unstated material travel expectations;
and being remote in a country where the company has no entity, which creates an employment-classification
and tax problem you inherit.

**Employer of record for international remote.** If you are not in a country where the company has an
entity, you may be engaged as a contractor or through an employer of record. The consequences are real:
employment protections, benefits, paid leave, notice periods, and tax treatment may all be weaker or
absent, and your employment status may be less secure. Ask directly which entity employs you and in which
jurisdiction. A vague answer is important information.

**Visa and sponsorship — assess honestly.** *Type*: employment visas typically require employer
sponsorship and tie you to a specific role and employer; intra-company transfers differ and are often
better; independent work permits are strongest and hardest. *Track record*: how many people have been
sponsored successfully in the last two years — ask for a number. *Timing*: processes run from weeks to
many months; get the timeline in writing including your part and theirs, and know who pays for filings and
government fees. *Dependents*: whether family can accompany you and the mechanism. *Duration and
constraints*: permanent or temporary, whether tied to your role (moving roles internally may require a new
filing), and how long you have to leave if employment ends. *Long-term path*: green card or permanent
residency support, at what stage, and any legal-fee benefit. *Costs*: filing fees, legal fees,
translations, reimbursable or not. And *restrictions on your own activities*, since many visas limit
self-employment or outside work — read the terms.

**Sponsorship red flags.** Being asked to buy your own sponsorship — legitimate visa services exist, but a
company pressuring you to pay for a visa it is obliged to sponsor is a bad sign. "We will sponsor after
you prove yourself" — companies rarely retroactively sponsor. No timeline, no named process, no lawyer
contact. An offer contingent on visa approval with no stated remedy if denied: ask what happens to your
offer and your status if the visa is refused. Your status depending on a single employer in a weak market
for that employer.

**The correct sequence.** Have a specialist immigration lawyer review before you resign from anything.
Understand whether the company has a documented process, your timeline, and your fallback. Do not resign
until the process has a clear start date with the company — a filed application with a receipt is
meaningfully better than a promise.

**Equity with visa status.** Stock for non-citizens carries tax and reporting complications, including
forms and obligations that vary by status. Ask the equity administrator what they support and what
reporting you own, and get tax advice specific to your status. Also ask whether equity is granted at all
in your jurisdiction.

**The non-negotiable question.** "If the visa is delayed or denied, what is the status of my offer and
what are my options?" If they cannot answer, you have a hope, not a plan.

### 15.3.15 Resigning gracefully: the last two weeks and the alumni network

🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**

**Resignation mechanics.** Check your contract for the required notice period and whether it must be in
writing. Deliver notice in person or by email to your manager and HR, with a short professional letter
giving your last working day and thanks. Brief, positive, free of reasons. Reasons belong in a separate
private conversation if at all — never in the written resignation, and never as an announcement to
colleagues.

**The notice period.** Give what you are contractually required to give. Giving less to start faster is a
small gain for a real cost: the goodwill that produces your references, your alumni network, and future
help. If you have an urgent reason — health, family, safety — ask your manager and HR privately for a
shortened notice; it is granted more often than candidates expect, and far more often when asked directly
than when handled by simply not showing up.

**Do not burn bridges, in the specific ways that matter.** Do not trash the company, team, or manager to
anyone; assume your words reach them, and they often do. Do not take or forward anything proprietary — code,
documents, data, contacts. Do not use your last weeks to recruit your own team to your next employer: it is
a hostile act even when the company is not staying, and it is widely punished. Do leave working code in
good shape — finish or hand off your work, update documentation, write the runbook for whoever inherits
it. This is the strongest predictor of a good reference. Return all property — laptop, badge, keys,
credentials, cards — and get written confirmation. Complete exit paperwork and knowledge transfer, and keep
copies of what you sign.

**The handover is the reference.** Write a document listing what you owned, where it is, how it works,
what is fragile, and what is in flight, then give an oral walkthrough. People remember the colleague who
made their transition easy.

**The exit conversation.** Ask for feedback on your performance while you still have leverage to act on
it, and write it down. Ask about the reference process and who will be contacted, and correct factual
errors now — a wrong title or project description in a reference is expensive and much easier to fix now.

**Keep the relationships you want to keep.** Your manager, closest colleagues, and mentor are who will
speak for you in two years. Tell them the news yourself before it is announced, tell them the real reason
in confidence, and ask directly — "Will you write me a reference if I need one in a year?" Answers given
in advance are reliable; answers extracted later are not.

**The alumni network as a durable asset.** Keep the internal Slack channels, group chats, mailing lists,
and community accounts (community Slack usually keeps you after you leave). Stay in touch deliberately —
occasional messages, things they would find useful, congratulations. Go back and visit or speak to your
old team when invited; it costs an hour and keeps you in the group's memory. Offer help to your former
teammates when you can: that is what keeps a network warm and what people remember when they need a
referral. Do not use your old team for information about your new employer's confidential matters, and do
not bring your old employer's confidential information anywhere. The reverse also holds: your network does
not disappear when you leave, and most referrals and hiring information come from the outside.

**Non-compete and non-solicitation, once more.** Know exactly what you can and cannot do in your first
ninety days, and get legal advice if the clause is broad or your next role is adjacent. Do not bring your
old company's code, documents, or confidential information to your new job. If in doubt about whether
something is confidential, ask your lawyer, not your new employer.

**First-day preparation.** Confirm start date, equipment shipment, badge, accounts, and first-week
schedule. Bring the contacts you need. Re-read the team documentation. Do not start a big project in week
one; start conversations.

### 15.3.16 The first 90 days plan

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Why the first quarter determines the outcome.** Almost all engineers who fail at a new job fail in the
first quarter, and almost always for the same four predictable reasons: they did not learn the system fast
enough, did not build relationships, did not deliver anything visible, or were too quiet to find out what
mattered. A plan written now prevents all four.

**Days 1–30: listen and map.**
- *Systems map*: the main services, data stores, deploy pipeline, alerting, on-call rotation — written
  down. Read the docs and code; ask the most senior person on the team for a tour.
- *People map*: immediate collaborators, manager's peers, cross-team dependencies, skip-level. For each,
  learn what they own and what they need from you. Thirty-day informal conversations are cheap and define
  the next two quarters.
- *Understand success*: get your manager's explicit definition of 30/60/90-day and 12-month success, in
  writing if possible, then repeat it back and confirm.
- *Ship something small but real* — a bug fix, a small feature, a test, a documented fix. The purpose is
  completing the entire loop: understand, change, deploy, observe. You are learning the system, not
  contributing significant code.
- *Ask about constraints*: what is off-limits, what broke last time, what the team wishes it had done
  differently.
- *Set up your environment in week one*: every system, the alerting you own, the dashboards you need,
  deploy rights.

**Days 31–60: contribute and diagnose.**
- *Own a deliverable* with a 6–8 week scope you can complete. Not huge — a project that ships and
  demonstrates competence.
- *Diagnose something*: fix a recurring problem, reduce an alert, close a ticket category, improve a flaky
  area. Diagnosis is high-visibility, low-risk, and teaches the system's real state.
- *Ask for feedback around day 45* — mid-point, not year-end: "What should I keep doing, and what should
  I stop doing?"
- *Fill the gaps you found*: return to the systems and people maps and close the holes. Teams with no such
  map are why new hires are useless for months.
- *Join the team's rituals*: code review, design review, incident review. Learn the review norms by
  reviewing early and often.
- *One visible improvement with a metric*: a small metric reduction, a documented process, a documented
  migration path, a test suite that removes a class of bug.

**Days 61–90: own a domain and start compounding.**
- *Take ownership of a system or subsystem* with clear boundaries, and write down what you own.
- *Propose a larger change* — migration, redesign, performance project — in writing, naming the problem,
  options, risks, and phasing. Do not implement it unilaterally; write it and let the team react.
- *Extend your network* to adjacent teams and the wider organization; present at an internal tech talk or
  write an internal doc where the culture allows it.
- *Have the longer-term conversation* with your manager: level expectations, promotion timeline, what you
  want to be doing in a year, what you need from them.
- *Build on-call readiness*: shadow a shift before you are on it.
- *Give back*: mentor, review, fix something outside your immediate area.

**The 30/60/90 conversation with your manager.** Propose it yourself in week one. Most managers welcome it
because it removes ambiguity, and it is a strong seniority signal. Keep it as a living document updated
in your one-on-ones.

**What to avoid in the first 90 days.** Do not redesign anything before you understand why it is that way.
Do not lead with opinions about the stack in month one — listen first, you will be told the constraints. Do
not become the loudest voice in the room; volume early reads as inexperience. Do not fix things nobody
asked you to fix, however tempting — symptom fixes without understanding cause damage relationships. Do not
skip the boring parts: the deploy pipeline, the on-call rotation, the incident history; skipping them is
why new hires cannot be given real work. Do not vanish into your ticket queue; visible small wins beat
invisible throughput. Do not complain about your previous employer, even obliquely.

**Making the plan real.** Before your start date, write down the systems and people to map, the
deliverable, the diagnosis, the proposal, and the 30/60/90 checkpoints with dates. Bring it to week one
and reconcile it with your manager. People who arrive with a written plan get treated as owners from week
one, because they behave like owners from week one. A fill-in template is in the templates section.

```

Hi <name> — I saw <specific recent work: launch, post, talk, open-source release>.

project in one sentence, with a link>.

in <the domain>; if you're hiring or know someone who is, I'd welcome an introduction.
```

```
Subject: <role> — <domain> — <years> years
Hi <name> — <role> with <N> years in <domain>, currently at <company>. Most recent:
<headline outcome with a number or concrete scope>.

adjacent capability>. I'm looking for <target role> in <market>, <remote/hybrid/onsite>,
```

```
Subject: Thank you — <role> at <company>

<One new piece of value: a clarification I under-explained, a link, a thought I had after.>

```

### Post-rejection follow-up
```
Subject: After <company> — <role>
Hi <name> — thanks for the time and for the honest feedback. <One specific thing you will do
differently.>
I'd love to be considered for <future scope or team> when timing lines up. And if anyone else
on your side is hiring <skill>, I'd welcome an introduction.
```

### Networking / informational interview
```
Subject: 30 minutes on <team> at <company>
Hi <name> — <context line>. I'm <role> working on <domain>.
I'm not looking for a job right now / I'm exploring <adjacent area> and I'd value 30 minutes
on what <team> actually works on day to day. Happy to send a few questions in advance.
```
Always end an informational interview with: "Is there anyone you think I should talk to about
<adjacent team>?" — that question is what converts it into referrals.

### Cold outreach to an editor
```
Subject: Pitch — <specific, evidence-backed claim about X>
Hi <name> — I want to write about <X>, and the angle is that <the specific claim most write-ups
get wrong>. Supporting material: <a project, a benchmark with methodology, a migration I ran>.
Draft outline: <three bullets>. Previously published at <link>. Not pitching anything else —
happy to time it to a slot that suits you.
```

## Tracker Schema

Two tabs: `Pipeline` (one row per application) and `Metrics` (formulas).

**Pipeline columns.**

| Column | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| id | text | `COMPANY-role-YYYYMMDD` |
| company / role_title / level_scope | text | your read of the level |
| req_id_url / jd_url | text, link | re-apply, prepping |
| date_applied | date | velocity, timing |
| source | enum | referral / recruiter / board / cold / alumni / inbound |
| referrer / contact | text | direct lines beat portals |
| resume_variant | enum | backend-systems / data-ml / frontend-product / general |
| fit_score | 1–5 | set *before* applying |
| stage | enum | applied / screen / technical / onsite / offer / rejected / ghosted / withdrawn |
| stage_date_last | date | drives follow-up queue |
| days_in_stage | formula | `=TODAY()-stage_date_last` |
| next_action / due_date | text, date | **drives the daily work view** |
| followup_count | 0–3 | prevents over-following |
| rejection_stage / rejection_reason | enum, text | the diagnostic pair |
| market_note | text | band heard, level heard, team signals |
| screen_notes / tech_notes / onsite_notes | text | per-dimension scores 1–5 |
| salary_researched | text | low–high, with source and date |
| offer_base / offer_bonus_pct / offer_signon | number | |
| offer_equity_units / offer_equity_type | number, enum | RSU / option / none |
| offer_notes | text | clawback, start date, contingencies |
| reapply_date / archive | date, bool | filter closed rows out yearly |

**Metrics formulas.**
```
applications_this_week = COUNTIFS(stage_date_last, ">=" & this_monday)
screen_rate           = COUNTIFS(stage, "<>applied") / COUNTIFS(stage, "<>Withdrawn")
screens_by_source     = COUNTIFS(source, "referral", stage, "<>applied")
screen_rate_by_source = screens_by_source / COUNTIF(source, "referral")
offers_by_source      = COUNTIFS(source, "referral", stage, "offer")
median_cycle_days     = MEDIAN(days from applied to first stage advance)
```
Report weekly on one screen: applications, screens, onsites, offers, stage conversion, source mix,
fit-score calibration. Then pick the weakest transition and choose one experiment for the coming week.

**Dashboard rules.** Sort by `due_date` for the daily view, `stage` for the pipeline view. Flag
anything with `days_in_stage` past your own threshold — that is your follow-up queue. Flag `fit_score`
5 rows that have gone stale; those are your highest-value follow-ups.

## Negotiation Script Set

```
1. OPENING (recruiter call)      "Before specifics — how is the role scoped and leveled, and how is
                                  comp structured for that level? I want to compare the right things."
2. LEVEL ASK                     "Given the scope — owning X end to end with Y and Z as partners — my
                                  experience lines up with <L+1>. How does leveling work, and who would
                                  I need to convince? Here's the work that supports it: <2 examples>."
3. BAND DISCOVERY                "What does the approved range look like for this level, and where does
                                  my experience sit inside it? I'd rather optimize for the whole
                                  package than negotiate one line item."
4. RANGE ANSWER                  "For total cash I'm targeting the upper part of the band for this scope —
                                  call it <low>–<high>. For base specifically I'm at <number> and I
                                  have real flexibility on structure."
5. COMPETING OFFER (truth only)  "I have a written offer at <level> with <structure>, decision by
                                  <real date>. The scope here is what I care most about; the package is
                                  close to comparable. If you can move on the items below, I'd have
                                  difficulty declining."
6. THE PACKAGE ASK               "1. Base at <number>. 2. Initial grant of <N> shares sized to the level.
                                  3. Signing bonus of <amount> covering what I forfeit leaving now.
                                  4. Off-cycle comp review at <month> tied to scope.
                                  If base is fixed, I'm happy to move any of 2–4 instead."
7. SIGNING BONUS CASE            "The number is the one-time forfeiture: <pro-rated bonus> plus
                                  <unvested equity>, net of tax. An equivalent one-time equity grant
                                  works for me. Can you check with <approver>? I'll put it in writing."
8. TRADE                         "Base is fixed — understood. Would the company be open to <sign-on /
                                  one-time equity top-up / off-cycle refresh>? I'm flexible on <X>."
9. CLOSE                         "Based on <summarize package>, I'm in. Confirm in writing: base, bonus
                                  target, <N> <RSUs/options> vesting <schedule>, strike <price>,
                                  sign-on <amount> with <clawback>, title <X>, start <date>."
10. EXTEND A DEADLINE            "I have a decision point on <date> I need to honor. I'm close here. Can
                                  I have until <date>? I can give you my answer in writing within hours
                                  of that date so your team can use the time."
11. RECRUITER ADVOCATE REQUEST   "Would you take this to <HM/comp> for me? Here's the case in one
                                  paragraph: <scope>, <market evidence with dates>, <my results>,
                                  <the ask>, <my flexibility>. Forward it as-is if you like."
12. HM SCOPE CONVERSATION        "Two things about the role, not the money: where the scope lands on
                                  level, and where you expect this hire in twelve months. If the scope
                                  is what I described, what would it take to make the package match?"
13. DEGRADING GRACEFULLY         "I hear you — the band is where it is. Straightforward: that puts me
                                  below market for this scope, which is why I can't say yes today. Can
                                  you check one alternative — <specific>? If not, I respect it and I'll
                                  tell the other company I'm going with them."
14. DECLINING                    "I've decided to go with <company>. I wanted you to hear it from me
                                  first. Thanks for <specific thing>. If you need a <skill> person, call me."
```

## Offer Comparison Spreadsheet Layout

**Tabs:** `Inputs` · `Normalize` · `Benefits` · `Scenarios` · `3-Year` · `Decision`.

**Tab 1 — Inputs** (raw, as received; do not analyze here): company, level/scope, location/work model,
start date, base, target bonus %, equity type, equity units, strike, vesting schedule, cliff, sign-on
(+ clawback), other cash, refresh policy, treatment of unvested on termination, written deadline.

**Tab 2 — Normalize** (one row per offer; formula in the cell comment).

| Line | Formula | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Base | input | | | |
| Bonus (yr 1) | `base × bonus% × (months/12)` | | | |
| Bonus (steady) | `base × bonus% × realism(0.8–1.0)` | | | |
| Sign-on + other cash (yr 1) | `input × (1 − t_one_time)` | | | |
| **Year-1 cash, net** | sum | | | |
| COL index to your city | `=index(you)/index(city)` | | | |
| **Base, COL-adjusted** | `base × COL index` | | | |
| Share price used | input + date | | | |
| RSU value/unit | `=share price` | | | |
| Option value/unit | `=MAX(0, price − strike) × p(in-the-money)` | | | |
| Gross equity at full vest | `units × value/unit` | | | |
| Vesting factor yr 1 | `=0.25` (4 yr monthly, mid-year start ≈0.19) | | | |
| Tax at vest | `× (1 − t_vest)` | | | |
| Liquidity / time discount | mature RSU 0.85; startup 0.3–0.5 | | | |
| P(outcome) | startup: your estimate | 1.0 | 1.0 | |
| **PV equity (2–3 yr)** | product of the above | | | |
| **Year-1 total, normalized** | cash + PV equity + benefits | | | |
| **3-year total** | roll forward w/ refresh + 1 promo | | | |

**Tab 3 — Benefits** — annual dollars, only what you will use: employer health contribution for *your*
plan and family status; retirement match as % of salary; paid leave (days × (base+bonus)/working days);
public holidays; parental leave (weeks × rate); equipment/remote budget; learning budget; on-call
compensation; relocation after tax if you will stay past the minimum; legal fee benefit. **Total row.**

**Tab 4 — Scenarios** — the sensitivity that matters: share price at −30%, base, +30%, and +100% only
if credible; multiply through equity PV and the 3-year total for each offer.

**Tab 5 — 3-Year** — per offer: Year / base (with one promotion) / refresh units / equity value /
benefits / total / cumulative. Then repeat for share price −30% and for "I leave at month 18" (only
vested equity counts).

**Tab 6 — Decision** — filled in *before* you negotiate:
```
Expected 3-year total (normalized):        $___
Confidence range:                            $___ – $___
Non-monetary factor I will trade money for: <scope | manager | mission | stability | growth>
Chosen offer and why (one paragraph):        ___
```

**Use in this order:** Inputs → Normalize → Benefits → Scenarios → 3-Year → Decision. Writing the
Decision tab first stops you negotiating toward a number instead of toward the outcome you chose.
