# PHASE 15 WORKED EXAMPLES

All figures are illustrative constructions, not real offers from real companies. They show the
arithmetic. Substitute your own numbers, and never cite these as market data.

Shared assumptions: combined tax + vesting withholding `t = 30%`; one-time payments taxed at 35%;
bonus realism factor `0.9`; liquidity/time discount on mature public RSUs `0.85`; refresh = 25% of
the initial grant, 4-year monthly vest; 250 working days per year.

## Example 1 — RSU-heavy vs cash-and-title-heavy (mature vs late-stage private)

**Candidate.** Staff-level backend engineer, 9 years, one time zone shift.

| | **Offer A** (large public, hybrid) | **Offer B** (late-stage private, remote) |
|---|---|---|
| Title / level | Staff / L5 | Senior Staff (director-level, no people mgmt) |
| Base | 240,000 | 275,000 |
| Target bonus | 15% | 10% |
| Equity | 22,000 RSUs @ $58 | 30,000 options, strike $2.10 |
| Sign-on / other | 20,000 | 35,000 + 10,000 relocation |
| Health | 18,000 (family) | 9,000 (employee only) |
| Match | 50% of first 6% = 3% | 4%, 3-year cliff |
| PTO | 20 days + 9 holidays | "unflexible" (price at ~12 used days) |

**Step 1 — year-1 cash.** A: `240,000 + 240,000×0.15 + 20,000×0.65 = 289,000`.
B: `275,000 + 275,000×0.10 + 45,000×0.65 = 331,750`. Raw cash favors B by 42,750.

**Step 2 — cost of living.** New-city COL index 118 vs current 100.
`A base, COL-adjusted = 240,000 × 118/100 = 283,200` vs `B = 275,000`. **The ordering flips** —
A was never lower; it was a higher-COL city with a lower nominal base.

**Step 3 — equity (the decisive step).**
```
A (RSU):  value/unit = 58.00;  yr-1 vested 22,000×0.25 = 5,500 sh
          5,500 × 58 = 319,000 × (1−0.30) = 223,300 × 0.85 = 189,805  ≈ 189,800
B (option): intrinsic = max(0, 2.10 − 2.10) = 0.00
          The grant is exactly at the money. 30,000 units is NOT 30,000 shares of value.
          Illustrative long-dated option approximation:
          0.40 P(in the money) × 0.60 spread × (1−0.30) = 0.168 per option
          yr-1 vested 7,500 × 0.168 = 1,260 × 0.50 (private illiquidity) ≈ 630
```
A's equity is worth ~**$189,800** for the year; B's ~**$630**. This is the entire decision.
**Insight:** never compare unit counts across offer types; never normalize an option count against an
RSU count.

**Step 4 — benefits, annualized.**
```
A: health 18,000 + match 240,000×0.03 = 7,200 + PTO 20 × (276,000/250 = 1,104) = 22,080
   + holidays 9 × 1,104 = 9,936                                    → 57,216
B: health 9,000 + own plan ~9,000 = 18,000 + match 0 in yr 1 (3-yr cliff)
   + 12 × (302,500/250 = 1,210) = 14,520                          → 32,520
```

**Step 5 — year-1 totals.**

| Line | A | B |
|---|---|---|
| Cash | 289,000 | 331,750 |
| Equity (net, discounted) | 189,800 | 630 |
| Benefits | 57,200 | 32,500 |
| **Year-1 total** | **536,000** | **365,000** |

**Step 6 — three-year view (with A promoted at month 18).**
```
A: Yr1 523,000 | Yr2 262,000 base + 39,300 bonus + 189,800 equity + 62,600 benefits = 571,700
   Yr3 265,500 + 31,860 + 189,800 + 62,600 = 553,760   → 3-yr ≈ 1,648,400
   at share price −30% ($40.60): equity/yr = 5,500×40.60×0.595 = 132,838 → ≈ 1,504,900
B: cash (302,500×2.5) + 29,250 = 835,500; benefits 32,500×2.5 = 81,250 → ≈ 916,750
   Upside case (3× last round, 4M preferred at 1× $2.10 = 8.4M preference, 15M FD post-money):
     exit 60M − 8.4M = 51.6M / 15M = 3.44/sh → intrinsic 1.34 × 30,000 = 40,200
     × 0.70 tax × 0.50 illiquidity = 14,070 → 3-yr ≈ 930,820
```
**Verdict.** Even in B's upside case it is roughly 700,000 worse over three years. The right
negotiation for B is not about base; it is a meaningful signing bonus, an above-market refresh in
writing, and confirmation of the strike and share count. **Lesson:** the first question to ask about
any option grant is the strike and the current share price.

## Example 2 — Startup equity, probability-weighted

**Candidate.** Senior engineer, 7 years, data/infra, currently at a mid-size public company.

| | **Offer S** (seed/Series A) | **Offer P** (stable private) |
|---|---|---|
| Base | 205,000 (below market) | 228,000 |
| Bonus | None | 10% |
| Equity | 180,000 options, strike $1.40 | 9,000 RSUs |
| Sign-on | 10,000 | 15,000 |
| Refresh | None stated — ask | Not stated |

**Dilution analysis.**
```
FD shares now              = 12,000,000   your 180,000 = 1.50%
Pool authorized 2,000,000; granted 900,000; unallocated 1,100,000
Next primary round         =  3,000,000
future FD = 12,000,000 + 1,100,000 + 3,000,000 = 16,100,000
your future %              = 180,000 / 16,100,000 = 1.12%
relative dilution          = (1.50 − 1.12)/1.50 = 25%
```
**You lose a quarter of your ownership to hiring and the next round, independent of performance.**

**Scenario analysis.** Assumptions stated so they can be challenged: downside 60% (no liquidity event),
base 25% (2× current price, year four), upside 15% (6×, year five). Preferred: 7,000,000 shares, 1×
non-participating, $1.40.

```
Downside:  $0

Base (exit = 2 × 1.40 × 12,000,000 = 33.6M):
  preference 7,000,000 × 1.40 = 9,800,000
  remaining  = 23,800,000 / 16,100,000 FD = 1.478/sh
  intrinsic  = max(0, 1.478 − 1.40) = 0.078
  gross 180,000 × 0.078 = 14,040 × 0.70 tax = 9,828 × 0.50 illiquidity = 4,914

Upside (exit = 100.8M):
  remaining = 100.8M − 9.8M = 91.0M / 16.1M = 5.652/sh → intrinsic 4.252
  gross 180,000 × 4.252 = 765,360 × 0.70 = 535,752 × 0.50 = 267,876

EV = 0.60×0 + 0.25×4,914 + 0.15×267,876 = 0 + 1,228 + 40,181 = $41,410
```
**Expected value of the "180,000 options" ≈ $41,000** — not $250,000, and not "180,000 units."

**Comparison.**
```
S yr-1 cash = 205,000 + 10,000×0.65 = 211,500
P yr-1 cash = 228,000 + 22,800 + 15,000×0.65 = 260,550
P's cash advantage in yr 1 = 49,050; over 3 yrs (ignoring raises) ≈ 122,600
P's equity is RSU-based, so it actually delivers: 9,000 × ~1.00 (P's private share value)
S's expected equity = 41,410 in expectation, 60% of the time zero.
```
**P beats S by roughly 80,000–120,000 in expected value over three years, before counting that P's
equity is a promise rather than an option.**

**Correct negotiation for S** — leverage is in cash, not shares:
```
1. Base to 225,000 (they almost certainly have room; this is the biggest lever)
2. Signing bonus 30,000 to bridge the base gap and forfeited bonus
3. Evergreen refresh clause (strike re-set every 12 months) — the single most valuable long-dated
   option term, and many companies will agree to it
4. Written refresh policy by level, since none is stated
5. Confirm the 409A refresh schedule — a low 409A lowers your exercise tax basis now
```
If they move 20,000 of base, accept and take the option as free upside. Do not trade a below-market
base for a large unit count.

## Example 3 — Level negotiation: a mid-level offer re-leveled upward

**Situation.** 7 years of experience; recruiter opens at L4 / mid-level. This compounds for years.

**Step 1 — get the scope in writing.**
```
Asked:   "What does this role own in its first year?"
Answer:  "You'll own <service> end to end, plus design for <adjacent area>, with two engineers as
          partners, and you'll be a reviewer on <larger area>."
```
End-to-end service ownership plus design authority over an area plus review authority across a larger
area is L5 work at most companies, regardless of title.

**Step 2 — the framing.** Note what this does: it never says "I deserve more money." It disputes the
*level of the job*, which is set by a calibration process driven by the hiring manager, not the
recruiter.
> "I'm going to be direct: I'm being offered L4, and I want to flag that the scope described is L5 work
> at the companies I know. Concretely: end-to-end ownership including <X>, design authority over <Y>,
> and review responsibility across <Z> — plus the background I mentioned, where I did <the equivalent>
> at <current company>. I'm not asking to skip a level. I'm asking whether this role is leveled
> correctly. If it can move to L5, I want to work there. If the company genuinely wants L4 scope, I
> want to know now so we're both clear."

**Step 3 — the response branches.**
- *Manager agrees and re-levels:* the whole package re-bases. Illustrative, where each level is ~15–20%
  on base and ~1.7× on the initial grant at $58/share:
  ```
  L4: base 195,000 | grant  9,000 × 58 = 522,000 | 10% bonus
  L5: base 225,000 | grant 15,000 × 58 = 870,000 | 15% bonus
  yr-1 delta = 30,000 base + 6,750 bonus + (6,000 × 58 × 0.70 × 0.85 = 207,096) = 243,846
  3-yr delta > 700,000, because refreshes are sized off level too.
  ```
- *Manager says the scope is L4:* then the scope needs reducing to L4. Do not accept L4 scope labelled
  L5 in the title.
- *Manager says the level is fixed but "we can revisit in six months":* get it in writing, with criteria.
  Promotions require scope evidence you have not yet had, so this is usually a deferral, not a
  commitment — price it accordingly at close to zero in the comparison.

**Step 4 — write it down.** Every agreement about level, scope, and review timing, in an email, so
"we'll revisit" has a written referent.

**The generalization:** the single most valuable negotiation in most searches is the level, not the
base. It is available only before the offer is written, and never again once you have accepted a
lower-level title.

## Example 4 — Full multi-offer normalization, including the work-model adjustment

**Candidate.** 11 years, senior level, two cities under consideration, three live offers.

| | **A** (large private, pre-IPO) | **B** (mid public, remote US-only) | **C** (large public, onsite) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Level / model | L5, hybrid 3 days | L4, remote | L5, onsite, downtown |
| Location (COL) | City A (100) | City B (96) | City A |
| Base | 250,000 | 215,000 | 265,000 |
| Bonus | 12% | 10% | 15% |
| Equity | 14,000 RSU @ $31 | 8,000 RSU @ $31 | 20,000 RSU @ $31 |
| Sign-on | 15,000 | 25,000 | 30,000 |
| Health | family 21,000 | employee only 8,000 | family 19,000 |
| Match | 4% / 1-yr vest | 5% / 3-yr cliff | 4% / 1-yr vest |
| PTO | 18 days + 9 hol | 15 days + 10 hol | 12 days + 9 hol |

**Year-1 cash** (one-time items × 0.65):
`A = 250,000 + 30,000 + 9,750 = 289,750` · `B = 215,000 + 21,500 + 16,250 = 252,750` ·
`C = 265,000 + 39,750 + 19,500 = 324,250`.

**COL normalization:** `A 250,000` · `B = 215,000 × (100/96) = 223,958` · `C 265,000`.

**Equity** (25% vested yr 1, × 0.70 tax, × 0.85 discount):
`A 3,500×31 = 108,500 × 0.595 = 64,558` · `B 2,000×31 = 62,000 × 0.595 = 36,890` ·
`C 5,000×31 = 155,000 × 0.595 = 92,225`.

**Benefits, annualized** (daily rate = (base+bonus)/250):
```
A: 21,000 + 250,000×0.04 = 10,000 + 18×1,120 = 20,160 + 9×1,120 = 10,080   → 61,240
B:  8,000 + 0 (3-yr cliff, not vested yr 1) + 15×946 = 14,190 + 10×946 = 9,460 → 31,650
C: 19,000 + 265,000×0.04 = 10,600 + 12×1,219 = 14,628 + 9×1,219 = 10,971   → 55,199
```

**Totals.**

| | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Year-1 cash | 289,750 | 252,750 | 324,250 |
| Year-1 equity (net) | 64,558 | 36,890 | 92,225 |
| Benefits | 61,240 | 31,650 | 55,199 |
| **Year-1 total** | **415,548** | **321,290** | **471,674** |
| COL-adjusted base | 250,000 | 223,958 | 265,000 |

**The work-model adjustment (where the decision changes).** City A commute averages 45 min one way;
3 days × 48 weeks = 144 days × 1.5 h = **216 hours/year** ≈ 27 working days. Valued at A's daily rate
that is ~**$30,000/yr of life** — 216 hours that cannot be spent with family, exercising, or learning.
`A adjusted = 415,548 − 30,000 = 385,548` · `B = 321,290` · `C = 471,674` (12-minute downtown office).

**Three-year roll-forward** (base +5%/yr, one promotion at month 20 for A and C = +12% base and 1.6×
grant; refreshes at 25% of initial grant vesting in years 2 and 3):
```
A  Yr1 415,548 | Yr2 = 262,500 + 31,500 + (64,558+64,558) + 65,000 = 488,116
   Yr3 = 265,500 + 31,860 + 129,116 + 65,500 = 491,976   → 3-yr ≈ 1,395,640 → less ~60,000
      commute value ≈ 1,335,640
B  Yr1 321,290 | Yr2 = 225,750 + 22,575 + (36,890+36,890) + 46,000 (match now vests) = 368,105
   Yr3 = 237,040 + 23,704 + 73,780 + 47,000 = 381,524   → 3-yr ≈ 1,070,919
C  Yr1 471,674 | Yr2 = 265,000 + 39,750 + (92,225+92,225) + 57,000 = 546,200
   Yr3 = promo yr: base 296,800 + 44,520 + (92,225+92,225+8,000×31×0.595=147,560) + 60,000
         = 825,555                                              → 3-yr ≈ 1,843,429
```
**Sensitivity at share price −30% ($21.70).** Equity is ~24% of C's three-year total, so the hit is
~7%: `C ≈ 1,714,000` · `A ≈ 1,255,500` · `B ≈ 1,006,600`. **The ranking is stable under the sensitivity
that matters** — which is what makes the decision defensible: the answer does not depend on the
assumption you are least sure about.

**Non-monetary adjustments, made explicit.**
```
A  + L5 at a pre-IPO company: refresh grants may be structured well and the company is about to have
    a liquid, marked share price — real optional upside on a company you evaluated.
    − 27 days/yr of commute. − hybrid policy can change after you start.
B  + fully remote, best autonomy, US-only constraint. − one level down (compounds).
    − 3-yr cliff on the match. − equity ~57% of A's per year. − no city choice beyond the US.
C  + highest total, fastest promotion path, downtown office (12 min), weakest leave of the three.
    − onsite = least flexibility about where you live. − most concentrated bet on one stock.
```

**The decision.** C wins on money, and survives sensitivity analysis — but only after checking three
things worth more than money:
1. **Is the 12-day PTO real?** Ask the team what people actually take. If it is 12, ask for 15–18;
   leave is cheap to grant and often traded for small concessions elsewhere.
2. **What are the L6 promotion criteria?** A three-year model that assumes a promotion is only worth
   counting if the promotion is achievable.
3. **Is 20,000 in-band for L5?** If it is an exception, exceptions at entry are sometimes revisited at
   the first review — confirm in writing either way.

**Negotiation plan for C.**
```
1. Level framework and promotion criteria confirmed in writing (governs the three-year model)
2. Initial grant band confirmed; if 20,000 is above band, secure it in writing
3. PTO 12 → 15 (cheap; cash equivalent ≈ 3,700/yr at their daily rate)
4. Sign-on 30,000 → 40,000, justified by pro-rated bonus + forfeited equity
5. Base +5,000, only if 1–3 are exhausted
Leverage: "I have a live written offer at <A's level and structure> with a decision on <date A>, and an
earlier deadline at B. The scope here is my preference, so a decision is easy if the package is right."
```
**What not to do:** do not negotiate all three to the maximum simultaneously. Settle C's items 1–3,
accept C if it lands, and use A as a reference rather than as a bidding chip at every stage.

# PHASE 15 INTERVIEW Q&A (30 questions with model answers)

**1. 🟢 Why are you leaving your current role?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
Forward-looking, never a complaint. "My work here has been good — I own X and I've learned Y. But over
the last year it has moved toward maintenance rather than the design work I want more of, and I've hit
the ceiling on what I can learn. I'm looking for a role where I'd be designing and shipping new systems,
with a team where that's the primary job." Never disparage, never hint at a conflict, never mention
compensation.

**2. 🟢 Why should we hire you?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
Shape the answer to the role's top three requirements. "Three things. First, I've done the exact
problem this role owns — at <company> I took <X> from <state> to <state> with <metric>. Second, the part
you're least staffed for is <dimension>, and that's where I've spent the last <N> years. Third, I work
the way your team works — <evidence from the posting>. Here's the project I'd point you to for each."

**3. 🟢 Tell me about yourself.** 🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**
60–90 seconds: present → relevant past → why here. "I'm a backend engineer, seven years, mostly
distributed systems and data infrastructure. Most recently at <company> I own <service>, where I <one
headline outcome>. Before that I <most relevant earlier role and outcome>. I'm applying because
<specific reason tied to this role>." Do not recite your resume; start with education only if
early-career.

**4. 🟢 Tell me about the most impactful thing you've done.** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
One project with depth: problem and why it mattered, what you chose and what you rejected, what you
built, the result with numbers, and what you would do differently. "The most consequential thing I've
done is <project>. The problem was <X>, which cost us <cost>. The obvious approach was <A> and I
rejected it because <reason>. I built <B>. The result was <metric>, and the thing I'm proudest of is
<the part nobody asks about>." That last line separates a senior answer from a mid answer.

**5. 🟡 How do you handle disagreement with a technical decision?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
Build a case, not an ego. "First I check whether we actually disagree or just see it differently —
often it's a priority mismatch, not a factual one. Then I make the disagreement cheap: a prototype, or
a measurement that would settle it. If it's genuinely a values question — consistency versus
availability — I argue the tradeoff explicitly to the person who owns the decision and commit fully
once it's made. I've been wrong more than once, which is why I try to make my wrongness cheap to
detect before I commit a team to it."

**6. 🟡 How do you handle disagreement with your manager about priorities?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
"I'll raise it once, clearly, with a recommendation rather than a problem. If the answer is still
different, I commit and execute at full strength — my job is to make their decision succeed, not to win
the argument. What I won't do is silently withdraw, because that leaves them with a broken assumption.
I'll implement it and say privately, 'I want to flag one risk so it isn't a surprise.'" Then a real
example with a good outcome.

**7. 🟡 What questions do you have for us?** 🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**
Always have three or four ready and specific: "What does success look like for the first six months?"
/ "What's the hardest technical problem the team has right now, and how much of my time would go to it?"
/ "How is on-call staffed, and what does a typical on-call week look like?" / "What's the team's
biggest source of internal disagreement right now?" / "What happened to the last person in this role?"
Never ask something you could answer from their website.

**8. 🟡 How do you decide what to work on?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
"I look for the intersection of user pain, business leverage, and something the team can finish. The
failure mode is optimizing for what's interesting to me, which is rarely what the business needs. In
practice: who is hurting, what does it cost them, and what's the smallest version that tells us whether
this is worth more. Then I bias toward work with a visible feedback loop, because work without a signal
is how teams disappear."

**9. 🟡 How do you handle an incident you're on call for?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
"Stabilize first, diagnose second, write it up third. Acknowledge, then decide whether to roll back —
my default is yes if the cause is unclear and the change is recent — communicate to the affected team
within a stated interval, and keep a real-time log because I'll need it. Then I hold every ten minutes
until the signal is clean, and I escalate only if the blast radius exceeds my authority. Afterwards I
write a blameless review with one page of actions with owners and dates, and I check that the actions
aren't the ones we already knew." Give a real example with the outcome.

**10. 🔴 How do you evaluate whether a technical decision was right, after the fact?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"I look for whether the decision still holds under the conditions we now know about, not whether it hit
the original number. Did the load change? Did we learn the user behavior we assumed? Would I re-make it?
And if not, what specifically broke — the assumption, the estimate, or the execution? That distinction
matters, because only the first two are things better analysis would have fixed." Give an example of a
decision that was wrong and one that was right.

**11. 🟡 What separates a good engineering manager from a bad one?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
You are interviewing your future boss, so answer as someone who has been on both sides. "A good one makes
the work legible — you can tell what matters this quarter and why, and you get early warning when it
changes. They convert ambiguity into decisions instead of handing it down. They take responsibility
upward so you can focus. And they give specific feedback about your work rather than general impressions.
A bad one manages for visibility instead of outcomes, or avoids the hard conversations and lets problems
surface in reviews. The most reliable signal I use is whether people on their team volunteer for hard
projects."

**12. 🔴 How do you make technical decisions in a group?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"I write the decision down before the meeting — problem, constraints, options, my recommendation with
reasoning, and what would make me wrong. That document does most of the work, because disagreement in a
meeting is usually about framing, not options. Then I name a decider up front, so we're solving the
problem rather than testing whose argument wins. If there's no consensus I stop arguing: I make the
call, record the reason, and set a review trigger — a metric or a date — so the decision is falsifiable
instead of permanent."

**13. 🔴 How do you handle a project that is failing?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"Separate diagnosis from morale. First, get the facts on the timeline — when did we last have evidence
this was going to work? Then identify the class of failure: is the premise wrong, the estimate wrong, or
the execution wrong? Those have completely different responses. Then take a decision to the people
involved early, with a recommendation, because the worst outcome is a team that knows it's failing and
hasn't been told. I would rather cut scope by half and ship in two weeks than keep a full-scope plan
that misses by a year."

**14. 🔴 Your testing philosophy, and where do you disagree with the orthodoxy?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"I test behavior, not implementation, because implementation-coupled tests make refactoring expensive
and don't tell you whether the system works. I push hardest for tests at boundaries — input validation,
error paths, concurrency, failure injection — because that's where bugs are. Where I'd push back on
orthodoxy: coverage as a target creates the illusion of safety, and mocking every collaborator produces
a suite that passes while the system fails. Integration tests with real dependencies are slower and catch
more." Give a concrete example of a test that caught a real bug.

**15. 🔴 How do you think about technical debt?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"Debt is only debt if it has a cost that arrives later, and interest is paid in delivery speed — so the
question is always whether we're buying something. I'd rather have a system I understand with known
limitations than one I don't. I want a cost model: what does this slow down, by how much, and what would
fixing it cost. If two weeks of work removes two days from every future change, do it. If it's a quarter,
it needs a triggering event to justify it." Mention one debt you paid down and how you prioritized it.

**16. 🔴 How do you decide what to build versus buy?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"I build when the thing is core to our differentiation, when we need to change it frequently, or when no
external option meets a hard requirement. I buy when the problem is solved well by someone whose full-time
job is solving it and I can absorb the integration cost. The failure modes are symmetric: building
something nobody wanted, and buying something we then fight constantly because we don't control the
roadmap. I also price the exit — the cost of replacing it later is part of today's decision."

**17. 🟡 How do you give and receive feedback?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
"I try to make feedback specific and close to the event — behavior, observed, impact — and I'd rather
hear something uncomfortable early than useful and late. As a receiver I ask 'what did you expect?' and
treat the gap between expectation and result as the actual feedback, not the conclusion. The failure mode
I work on is that when I'm tired or defensive I hear the conclusion and ignore the reasoning." Give a
real example of feedback you received that changed your behavior, and one you gave that landed.

**18. 🟡 How do you stay current in your field?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
"I have three filters. I follow a small number of people whose work I respect, I read the primary source
— design docs, RFCs, post-mortems — rather than the summary, and I try to apply what I read to something
within a couple of weeks, because reading without application doesn't stick. I'd rather go deep on one
new thing a quarter than skim ten." Be honest about what you currently read; vagueness is a red flag.

**19. 🔴 Tell me about a time you missed a deadline or shipped something that failed.** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
An integrity question. "I committed to <X> by <date> and missed it. Here's what happened: <cause,
without blaming>. Here's the recovery I did: <honest recovery>. Here's what I changed: <system change>."
Then what you learned about estimating. A candidate who has never missed a deadline is either very new
or not being honest. Do not offer a disguised strength.

**20. 🔴 Tell me about a time you were wrong about a technical judgment.** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
Give a specific position, why you held it, the evidence that changed your mind, what it cost, and what
you do now. "I argued we didn't need to shard <service> until <number> users. I was wrong — the cost
wasn't write throughput, it was the operational complexity of migrations we had to do by hand. What I
took from it: I now distinguish 'scaling limits' from 'operational limits', because they have different
solutions, and I check for the second when I look at a system's growth."

**21. 🟡 Why are you at the level you're at, rather than the one above?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
The best signal you can give a senior interviewer. "The next level for me is <scope across teams,
leading a migration, owning a roadmap>. What I have is <specific evidence>. What I don't have yet is
<specific, honest>. If you hire me for the level above, here's what I'd do in the first six months to
earn it — <plan>." Candidates who claim they already operate at the level above are routinely filtered
out in the calibration conversation afterwards.

**22. 🔴 How would you scope and staff a 30-person, 6-month project?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"First I'd find out whether the six months is real, because I'd rather negotiate the scope than discover
in month five that the date was aspirational. Then define the one outcome that makes this successful if
everything else slips, and build toward that first so we have something shippable by week eight. On
staffing, I'd want two or three people who know the domain deeply and a couple who know the new
technology, deliberately paired, and a dedicated point person for coordination rather than assuming a
senior engineer picks it up. And I'd plan the last two weeks for hardening and rollout, because that's
where every project I've watched slip decided its outcome." Then a real project and what happened.

**23. 🔴 Your system is degrading. What do you do in the first hour?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"Minute one: confirm what's actually happening and whether users are affected, using two independent
signals — a single dashboard can be lying. If users are affected I declare an incident and get a second
person on it immediately, because solo debugging is how an hour becomes three. The first three moves, in
order: check for a recent change, check whether a dependency is degraded, check whether it's capacity or
correctness. Those three cover most causes. Everything after that is diagnosis, and I'll be explicit in
updates about what I don't know rather than guessing. I'll also set the rollback criteria before I need
them." Then a real example and the actual cause.

**24. 🔴 How do you handle a dependency you don't control?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
"Three stages. First, reduce the blast radius: timeouts, circuit breakers, retries with jitter and a
budget, bulkheads, and caching that respects their SLO rather than ours. Second, change what we ask for:
better terms, a dedicated path, a version, a deprecation notice. Third, plan for the worst: our
replacement or forked path, and how long it would take. The most common failure is spending all the
engineering effort on retries, which converts a dependency outage into our own outage — retries need
budgets specifically so a slow dependency can't consume our whole thread pool."

**25. 🟡 What salary are you looking for?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
Never answer first if you can avoid it: "Can I ask how the band is structured for this level, and where
my experience lands in it? I'd rather get the whole package right." If forced, give a range at the top
of what is credible, anchored to scope and market, with the reasoning attached: "For this scope I expect
<L+1>, and for total cash in the <X–Y> range. I'd have flexibility on structure." Then stop talking.
Never name your current salary.

**26. 🟡 What's your biggest weakness?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
Real, non-fatal, with a demonstrated mitigation. "I used to over-invest in getting a design perfect before
showing anyone — I'd hold a proposal for weeks. What I do now is show work in progress deliberately
early, at a level where I ask for direction rather than approval, because I got burned by a design I was
proud of that solved a problem nobody had." Avoid the "I work too hard" lie and disguised strengths. Be
ready for "tell me about a time."

**27. 🔴 Why should we not hire you?** 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**
Integrity and self-awareness; a bad answer sinks a strong candidate. "Two reasons someone might decide
against me. I sometimes over-index on the technical depth of a solution and under-invest in the social
work of getting people behind it — I've learned to do that deliberately and early, and to ask for help.
And my background is <domain>, so in <adjacent domain> I'd be learning for the first few months where
someone with <domain> experience would be productive day one. If this role needs day-one productivity
in <adjacent domain>, I might not be right. If it needs someone who reaches production quality fast in
<domain>, I would." Then what you would do to fix each.

**28. 🔴 What do you want to be doing in three years?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
Tie it to the role and to real scope. "I want to be leading a system or area where I'm responsible for
design across more than one team, and being the person people come to when the hard design question is
<your domain>. I'm not in a rush to manage people — I've done it and I'm good at it, but I'd rather go
deep a couple more years and then decide." Then connect it: "That's why I'm talking to you, because
<specific reason>."

**29. 🟡 Why this company?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
Never answer about mission generically. Use one of three real reasons: a specific technical problem you
want to be near, a domain you want deeper, or a constraint you find interesting rather than merely
acceptable. "I read your post on <specific technical thing> and hit a related version of the same problem
at <current company> — <the specific thing>. I'd like to be working on that class of problem rather
than one layer away from it. And the constraint that <their system has> is one I enjoy, because
<reason>." Finish with something you want to learn from them specifically.

**30. 🔴 Anything you want us to know before we decide?** 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**
Close gaps, raise unmentioned evidence, or flag logistics. "Two things. First, I noticed your posting
asks for <X> — I haven't worked in production with it, but here's the adjacent thing I did do
<specific work>, and I'd pick it up fast; I'd rather you hear that from me than find out in week six.
Second, my availability is <date>, and I'm in the process at <other company> with a decision on <real
date>, so if there's timeline pressure I'd rather we plan around it openly."

# PHASE 15 RAPID-FIRE (45)

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | What does an ATS actually do? | Parses your resume into fields, indexes the text, and queries it — a database row, not a document. |
| 2 | Single column or two? | Single column for content; two-column header only. Multi-column content is the top parse risk. |
| 3 | One page or two? | One under ~10 relevant years, two above. Strongest content in the top third either way. |
| 4 | Why no dates? | Recruiters compute tenure and spot gaps. `Mon YYYY – Present` is standard. |
| 5 | Should I put pronouns? | Only if you want them and can defend them. A preference question, not a technical one. |
| 6 | What if I cannot quantify an achievement? | Use an ordinal claim with a basis: "cleared the internal SLO we previously missed at peak." |
| 7 | How many bullets per role? | 3–5 recent, 1–2 older, strongest first. |
| 8 | The bullet formula? | Strong verb + what you changed + how + measurable outcome. |
| 9 | Should I include every technology I've touched? | No. Only what you can be interviewed on — a longer list lowers your effective claim. |
| 10 | Highest-leverage resume edit? | Reordering so the target role's must-haves appear in the first third. |
| 11 | Is a summary worth it? | Yes, 3–4 lines naming role, domain depth, and two outcomes — if it answers the reader's next question. |
| 12 | How many resume versions? | Two or three written well, by domain framing, plus one generalist. |
| 13 | What does the filename matter? | Recruiters forward by name. `FirstnameLastname-Resume-<Role>.pdf` parses and sorts. |
| 14 | PDF or DOCX? | PDF, text-selectable, fonts embedded; verify with a copy-paste text test. |
| 15 | When do I send a cover letter? | Only with something specific the resume cannot say, or where a human will read it. |
| 16 | Which channel has the best conversion? | Warm channels almost always — but measure yours; your `source` field drives that. |
| 17 | Why do boards convert worse? | You're one of hundreds in a ranked pool, read by software first, against a throughput incentive. |
| 18 | Applications per week? | 20–30 while employed; 40–60 unemployed if you want a shorter timeline. Quality-adjusted. |
| 19 | Decent screen rate? | 10–20%. Below that, targeting and materials are the bottleneck, not interview prep. |
| 20 | Live processes needed? | Three to five concurrent late-stage processes. One option is a coin flip, not leverage. |
| 21 | No screens at all? | Fix targeting and resume variant. Check level mismatch and headline visibility. |
| 22 | Screens but no onsite? | Recruiter-screen performance: motivation, comp answers, timeline, and whether you ask questions. |
| 23 | Onsites but no offers? | Story coherence, references, level calibration, cross-functional breadth. |
| 24 | Follow-up frequency? | Once per meaningful stage plus one final check; two per process, not more. |
| 25 | Follow-up timing? | 7–10 days after applying, 1–2 after a round, same day after an onsite. |
| 26 | Recruiter or interviewer? | The recruiter. One point of contact per company, always. |
| 27 | What kills referrals? | Asking without a specific target and a one-line reason you fit. |
| 28 | Best referrers? | Former close colleagues, past hirers of your role type, adjacent peers, and your OSS/writing audience. |
| 29 | Networking while employed? | The highest-leverage thing you can do. Roughly five unasked-for interactions per ask. |
| 30 | What converts an informational interview? | Ending with "who else should I talk to about adjacent teams?" |
| 31 | Name my current salary? | Never. It anchors below market and reveals your minimum delta. |
| 32 | "What are you looking for?" | "What does the band look like for this level, and where do I fall in it?" |
| 33 | When do I anchor high? | With a real competing offer or strong specific market evidence — and attach the reasoning. |
| 34 | May I mention a competing offer? | Yes, if it is real. Never fabricate one; the details are verifiable. |
| 35 | Most valuable thing to negotiate? | Level/title — durable, re-bases everything, and only available before the offer is written. |
| 36 | Second most valuable? | Equity refresh policy — recurring value no year-one comparison shows. |
| 37 | Easiest component to move? | Sign-on or other one-time cash, from a separate approval pool. |
| 38 | Are counter offers worth it? | Usually no, unless the reason you wanted to leave is genuinely addressed. |
| 39 | Value startup options how? | Intrinsic × P(in the money) × (1 − tax) × illiquidity discount, then probability-weight scenarios. |
| 40 | What is a 409A? | An independent appraisal of fair market value used for employee share pricing — a tax basis, not a forecast. |
| 41 | Normalize two offers how? | Same units, date, and assumptions: cash after tax, equity net of vest tax and discounted, benefits you'll use. |
| 42 | What about vesting forfeiture? | If you might leave in 18 months, year-one value is roughly the vested portion. |
| 43 | What must I get in writing? | Level, base, bonus %, equity units/type/vesting/strike, sign-on and clawback, start date, contingencies. |
| 44 | Should I negotiate all live offers at once? | No. Settle your preferred one and use the others as references, not bidding chips. |
| 45 | What do I owe people I asked? | One brief follow-up with the outcome — and an ongoing relationship after you land. |

# PHASE 15 FINAL READINESS CHECKLIST

## Application materials
- [ ] Resume parses cleanly: text-extraction output is ordered, complete, unduplicated.
- [ ] Single-column body; no text boxes, header/footer content, or rules in content.
- [ ] Section labels conventional; dates `Mon YYYY`; no unexplained gaps.
- [ ] Every number sourceable, attributable, defensible; shared work labeled as shared.
- [ ] Titles match reality and LinkedIn; skills list only what you can be interviewed on.
- [ ] Strongest content in the top third; no page break mid-bullet.
- [ ] Two to three variants exist, mapped to framings, with a known variant per target role.
- [ ] LinkedIn headline, About, Featured, and skill order match the resume.
- [ ] GitHub profile README written; three repos pinned and presentation-ready.
- [ ] One project has a README with problem, architecture, decisions, and limitations.
- [ ] Personal site contains only what you would defend to an employer and to family.
- [ ] One positioning statement, written and reused everywhere.

## Funnel
- [ ] Tracker live with source, referrer, variant, stage, stage dates, next action, due date,
      rejection stage, rejection reason, fit score, reapply date.
- [ ] Funnel conversion computed stage-by-stage over the last 40+ applications.
- [ ] Weakest transition identified; one experiment chosen for this week.
- [ ] Weekly review scheduled and completed at least twice.
- [ ] Recruiter screen rehearsed: band discovery, range answer, closing question.
- [ ] Contacts list with "would refer me" and "have asked" columns; top 10 personalized.
- [ ] Three or more concurrent late-stage processes, or a plan to build that.
- [ ] Follow-up cadence defined and executed on every live process.
- [ ] Market research: 10–15 dated observations across three source types, normalized.
- [ ] Level mapping done against a common internal level framework.
- [ ] Gap narrative written: what happened, what you did, what you want, what you're ready for.

## Offer and negotiation
- [ ] Written offer received covering level, base, bonus, equity units/type/vesting/strike, sign-on and
      clawback, start date, contingencies.
- [ ] Level and scope confirmed, not just the number.
- [ ] Equity terms understood: units, strike, vesting, cliff, refresh policy, unvested on termination.
- [ ] Dilution estimated: FD shares, unallocated pool, your post-round percentage.
- [ ] Liquidation preferences modeled, if startup equity is involved.
- [ ] Refresh policy asked about explicitly and the answer recorded.
- [ ] Offers normalized in one spreadsheet, with a multi-year model and share-price sensitivity.
- [ ] Non-monetary factors (scope, manager, on-call, commute, reversibility) valued explicitly.
- [ ] Decision tab written before negotiating.
- [ ] Negotiation package prepared: ranked asks and a one-paragraph forwardable case.
- [ ] Extension script ready for a competing decision date.
- [ ] Employment agreement, IP assignment, and any non-compete requested in advance.
- [ ] Non-compete scope, duration, geography, compensation, and carve-outs reviewed.
- [ ] Prior-inventions list drafted for an IP schedule.
- [ ] Relocation: total value, tax treatment, clawback terms, minimum stay, carve-outs.
- [ ] Visa: sponsoring entity, jurisdiction, timeline in writing, dependents, long-term path.
- [ ] Health plan: deductible, out-of-pocket max, network, family cost, HSA status reviewed.
- [ ] Retirement match formula, caps, and vesting cliff understood; leave valued in dollars.
- [ ] First 90 days plan written, with systems map, people map, deliverable, diagnosis, 90-day measures.

## Closing and start
- [ ] Contract reviewed before signing; a lawyer consulted on anything unusual or material.
- [ ] Notice period confirmed and honored; written resignation brief, positive, reason-free.
- [ ] Handover document written and walkthrough scheduled.
- [ ] References confirmed with colleagues while still colleagues; titles and facts corrected.
- [ ] Company property returned, with written confirmation.
- [ ] Alumni plan: internal channels kept, relationships maintained, check-ins scheduled.
- [ ] First day logistics confirmed: equipment, accounts, badge, first-week schedule.
- [ ] Losing offers declined promptly, specifically, and graciously.

You now have the full search operating system: materials that survive parsing and get retrieved, a
funnel you can measure and therefore improve, and an offer-evaluation method that converts five
incommensurable numbers into one decision you can defend.

**The three things that actually determine the outcome, in order:**
1. **Targeting and channel mix** — where your applications come from dominates everything downstream,
   and it is a weekly choice, not a skill.
2. **Level calibration** — the level you are hired at re-bases base, equity, refresh, and every future
   raise. It is negotiated once, early, and it compounds for years.
3. **Concurrency** — three real alternatives is the precondition for negotiating at all.

**The three things that feel most important and are not:** how polished your resume template is, how
many jobs you apply to, and how impressive your negotiation scripts sound. All three matter; none is
where the leverage is.

**Carry forward.** The first 90 days plan you write during negotiation is the most durable artifact in
this phase — it determines whether the offer you agonized over turns into the career you wanted.
Negotiate the scope, not just the number.

# CROSS-CUTTING TRACKS

Projects, learning paths, role tracks, and level tracks. Every stage points back into this file,
so treat it as the spine: pick a project, pick a path, pick a role track, then calibrate level.

Conventions used throughout:

- Every project names concrete technologies. "A database" is not a requirement; "PostgreSQL 16
  with a migration tool" is.
- Every project separates must-have from stretch. Must-have is the interviewable core; stretch is
  what separates a shipped project from a tutorial clone.
- Every project has a rubric, so you grade yourself before an interviewer does.
- Difficulty labels: `🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**`, `🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**`,
  `🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**`, `⚫ Expert`. Unlabelled detail is supporting material.

Three rules make projects work. **Ship it somewhere real** — a deploy is a forcing function, and
the failures are the interview stories. **Write the README last and honestly** — a README that
lists what you never fixed is a stronger signal than one claiming production readiness. **Keep a
decision log** — one line per decision: what you chose, what you rejected, why. That file becomes
your best interview material and costs 30 seconds per entry.

Order if you follow stages: X.1.1 → X.1.2 → X.1.3 → X.1.4 → X.1.5 → X.1.6 → X.1.7 → X.1.8.
Changing tracks or returning from a break? Jump to the project matching your goal level and work
backwards.

---

## X.1 Projects (one per stage)

A project per stage is not portfolio decoration. It is spaced repetition: meet a concept in a
lecture, rebuild it under friction, then re-explain it out loud in an interview. Projects are
where the forgetting curve gets flattened.

---

### X.1.1 Responsive portfolio (HTML/CSS/JS)

**Why this project, and what it proves**

The smallest project that still exercises the whole browser rendering pipeline, and the one place
you have no excuse for hiding behind a framework. It proves you can write semantic HTML that
survives a validator and a screen reader; that you understand the box model, cascade, specificity,
and inheritance well enough to debug a layout without `!important`; that you can build responsive
layouts with fluid units instead of magic pixel breakpoints; and that you can ship — DNS, TLS,
env config, cache headers, a build step, a lighthouse score you can defend.

The interview story is unusually strong because it is verifiable. "My site scores 100 on
accessibility and performance" is checkable in thirty seconds, so this project returns more per
hour invested than any other on this list.

**Requirements**

*Must-have*

- 🟢 Semantic HTML5: `header`/`nav`/`main`/`section`/`article`/`footer`, one `h1`, no heading
  skips, `alt` on every meaningful image, a skip-to-content link.
- 🟢 Hand-written responsive layout: custom properties as a design token layer, `clamp()` for
  fluid type, grid and flexbox for structure, no fixed heights on text containers, media queries
  only where genuinely needed.
- 🟢 Dark/light themes via `prefers-color-scheme` plus a manual toggle persisted to
  `localStorage`, with all animation gated on `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- 🟢 Vanilla JS modules rendering three views from a data file: a project grid, a filter/search
  control, and a detail view. No framework.
- 🟢 Progressive enhancement — all projects, text, and contact links present in the HTML source,
  not injected by JavaScript.
- 🟢 Contact form validating on the client and posting to a real endpoint, with real loading,
  success, and error states.
- 🟢 Tooling and delivery: Vite, ESLint + Prettier, deployed to Netlify/Vercel/GitHub Pages or
  S3 + CloudFront with a real certificate.
- 🟢 Lighthouse 100/100/100/100 on the deployed URL, mobile-throttled.
- 🟢 `README.md` with the decision log, a live URL, and a screenshot.

*Stretch*

- 🟡 Static content pipeline: Markdown with front matter compiled to JSON at build time, so adding
  a project means adding a file.
- 🟡 Security headers in the host config: CSP, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`,
  `Permissions-Policy`.
- 🟡 Per-project real URLs via the History API, linkable and back-button correct.
- 🟡 `IntersectionObserver` reveal animations, disabled entirely under reduced motion.
- 🟡 Build-time Open Graph images, `sitemap.xml`, canonical URLs.
- 🔴 Hand-rolled fuzzy search over project metadata with a debounced, keyboard-navigable UI.

**Architecture**

- `index.html` — the semantic shell, containing the full static content fallback.
- `main.js` — entry module: imports views, wires the router, boots the theme.
- `data/projects.js` — the single source of truth: `slug`, `title`, `stack[]`, `year`, `summary`,
  `highlights[]`, `links`, `tags[]`.
- `views/grid.js` — renders the grid with `document.createElement`, never `innerHTML` with
  interpolated data.
- `views/detail.js` — one project by slug, updating `document.title` and the meta description.
- `lib/router.js` — ~40-line History API router: route table, `popstate`, a click interceptor
  that respects modifier keys and `target=_blank`, and focus management after navigation.
- `lib/theme.js` — `localStorage` → `matchMedia` fallback → sets `data-theme` on `<html>` before
  first paint via a sub-400-byte inline script.
- `lib/store.js` — ~30-line observable store (`subscribe`, `set`, immutable updates) used by the
  filter UI and the theme.
- `lib/dom.js` — the five functions you need: `el()`, `frag()`, `clear()`, `mount()`.
- `styles/{tokens,layout,components,utilities}.css` — tokens, structure, components, and only
  four utility classes.

Data model (JSDoc-typed so editors check it without a build step):

```js
/**
 * @typedef {Object} Project
 * @property {string} slug    kebab-case, unique, the route key
 * @property {string} title
 * @property {string} year
 * @property {string[]} stack  ordered most-important-first; first 3 render as chips
 * @property {string} summary  one sentence, max 140 chars, reused in meta description
 * @property {string[]} highlights  3 bullets, each starting with a verb
 * @property {{live?: string, repo?: string, writeup?: string}} links
 * @property {string[]} tags  used by the filter UI
 */
```

Request paths (static, so "request paths" means navigation and asset delivery):

1. **Cold load**: HTML (revalidated, `max-age=0, must-revalidate`) → CSS (immutable, hashed) → JS
   bundle (immutable, hashed) → font (subset, preloaded, `font-display: swap`). Critical CSS inlined
   under 14 KB. Nothing third-party in the critical path.
2. **Project detail**: `/projects/atlas-chat` → edge serves `index.html` via SPA rewrite → JS
   hydrates the route and updates title and meta. Accept the SEO limitation knowingly, or add a
   build-time static copy of each project's meta.
3. **Form submit**: `POST /api/contact` → rate limit → honeypot → serverless function →
   transactional email → 202 with a request id. Never echo the submitted address into the DOM
   unescaped.

**The hard parts**

1. **A 100 Performance score on mobile throttle.** Reserve every image's aspect ratio (`width` and
   `height` attributes), serve modern formats, inline critical CSS so first render does not wait on
   a stylesheet, and — the detail people miss — use a metric-adjusted fallback font:
   `@font-face { font-family: Fallback; src: local(...); size-adjust: 97%; ascent-override: ... }`
   with `font-display: swap`, so the swap does not shift layout. Then delete code; bundle analysis
   usually finds 30% you do not ship.
2. **A theme toggle that does not flash white at 2am.** A sub-400-byte inline script in `<head>`
   reads `localStorage`, falls back to `matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)')`, and sets
   `document.documentElement.dataset.theme` before the body parses. Every colour is a custom
   property redefined inside `[data-theme='dark']`; no component rule ever hardcodes a hex value.
3. **Rendering without a flash of empty content.** Build-time static markup for the default view,
   then adopt the existing DOM on boot rather than clearing it — hydrate by walking `[data-render]`
   markers. Avoid `opacity: 0` + `visibility: hidden` for the pre-hydration state; it breaks
   no-JS and confuses assistive tech. Use `content-visibility: auto` with `contain-intrinsic-size`
   for offscreen sections instead.
4. **A filter UI that stays at 60fps with 200 items.** Keep a `Map<slug, HTMLElement>` of rendered
   nodes and toggle a class or `hidden` instead of re-rendering; wrap card text in
   `content-visibility: auto`; debounce input at 120ms on the trailing edge; coalesce rapid changes
   into one `requestAnimationFrame` pass.
5. **A modal that is actually accessible.** Trap focus with `inert` on the rest of the tree,
   handle `Escape`, restore focus to the trigger on close, `role="dialog"` with `aria-modal` and a
   labelled title, and lock scroll without layout shift by setting `overflow: hidden` on
   `documentElement` and compensating with `padding-right: var(--scrollbar-width)`. All six details
   get probed.

**Milestones**

| # | Task | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| M1 | Scaffold + design tokens (colour, type, spacing, radii via `clamp()`) | 4h |
| M2 | Static semantic shell: all sections in HTML, validator clean | 4h |
| M3 | Responsive layout: header, about, grid, contact, footer, 320→2560 | 6h |
| M4 | Theming and motion: no-flash inline script, toggle, reduced motion | 3h |
| M5 | Data-driven grid + real detail routes from `data/projects.js` | 5h |
| M6 | Filtering and search: tag filter, text search, debounced, node reuse | 4h |
| M7 | Contact form: validation, POST, loading/success/error, honeypot | 3h |
| M8 | Accessibility pass: axe clean, full keyboard walkthrough, contrast | 4h |
| M9 | Performance pass: critical CSS, fonts, images, cache headers, Lighthouse | 4h |
| M10 | Deploy, security headers via `curl -I`, README + decision log | 3h |
| S | Stretch: Markdown pipeline, static meta, JSON resume export | 6h |

~44h core, ~6h stretch. At 8h/week, six weeks.

**Evaluation rubric**

0–3 per row, 30 total. Below 20: keep fixing. 26–30: genuinely competitive for any
frontend-leaning junior screen.

| Dimension | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Semantic HTML / a11y | div soup | landmarks, wrong headings | semantic and ordered, alt text | axe clean, keyboard complete, screen reader verified |
| CSS architecture | inline styles, `!important` | works, duplication | tokens, no magic numbers | tokens + primitives, zero leakage between components |
| Responsive craft | fixed px, breaks | media queries work | fluid units, clean 320→2560 | content-driven breakpoints, no scroll at any width |
| JS architecture | inline handlers, globals | one big file | ES modules, small functions, explicit state | store + router + views, no globals, tree-shaken |
| Performance | slow | assets unoptimised | hashed assets, lazy images | Lighthouse 100 mobile, inlined critical CSS, metric-adjusted fonts |
| Deployment & ops | localhost | deploy button | domain, HTTPS, headers | headers in config, CI deploy on push, decision log committed |

**What an interviewer probes**

- "Walk me through the critical rendering path" — expect HTML → render-blocking CSS → parser-
  blocking JS → first paint → lazy, and what you inlined and why.
- "How did you avoid a theme flash?" This separates people who shipped from people who copied.
- "Why `clamp()` over media queries?" Expect content-driven scaling, fewer breakpoints, no
  device-specific guessing.
- "How do you know it's accessible?" Automated tooling finds roughly a third of issues; the rest is
  a manual keyboard pass. An automated score alone is a warning sign.
- "What is your JS payload and what would you remove?" Expect a number in KB and at least one
  deletion candidate.

**Follow-on extension**

Build-time content pipeline so case studies are files; per-route analytics with one number and one
decision per page; `robots.txt`, `sitemap.xml`, canonicals, build-time OG images; a global error
listener swapping in a friendly message; documented cache headers with versioned assets and an
invalidation story; and a service worker only if you can state precisely what it buys a portfolio
(precached shell, network-first documents) — otherwise a deliberate omission is the better answer.

### X.1.2 To-do app with TypeScript and tests

**Why this project, and what it proves**

This is where most candidates claim competence and cannot demonstrate it. A to-do app looks
trivial until you require typed domain models, a state machine for task lifecycle, an audit trail of
transitions, and a test suite proving the reducer correct. It proves you use TypeScript as a design
tool — expressing the domain as discriminated unions and total functions so the compiler finds your
bugs; that you understand the unit/integration/e2e split and can write tests that fail for real
reasons rather than implementation details; that you can model stateful UI without a framework; and
that you can persist, migrate, and reason about failure.

The interview story is about *decisions*: why a union over five booleans, why one reducer, why the
tests test behaviour rather than markup.

**Requirements**

*Must-have*

- 🟢 `strict` mode plus `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`,
  `noImplicitOverride`. Zero `any`; `@ts-expect-error` only with a comment saying why the compiler
  is wrong.
- 🟢 A domain model that cannot be invalid: status as a discriminated union, not five booleans.
- 🟢 Create, inline edit, complete, delete, due date, priority, notes, filter, sort, search, and
  undo of the last destructive action.
- 🟢 `localStorage` persistence with a versioned schema (`{ version: 3, tasks: [...] }`) and one
  migration function per version.
- 🟢 A pure `(state, action) => state` reducer with no side effects and no `Date.now()` inside;
  time and randomness injected.
- 🟢 Undo as an inverse action log, not state snapshots.
- 🟢 Keyboard: `n` new, `/` search, `j`/`k` navigate, `e` edit, `x` toggle, `Enter` save,
  `Escape` cancel, `?` shortcut overlay.
- 🟢 Tests, in Vitest plus Playwright:
  - Unit: the full transition table, including invalid transitions.
  - Property-based, with `fast-check`: random action sequences asserting purity (deep-frozen
    input), no task lost, and undo restoring the exact prior state.
  - Integration: the repository against a real in-memory or mocked store, including v1 migration.
  - E2E: create-and-complete, filter-and-search, migrate-an-old-payload.
- 🟢 Honest coverage — 90%+ on the domain layer, with an explanation of what the uncovered lines are.
- 🟡 Accessibility: a real listbox pattern with `aria-selected`, live-region announcements for
  filter results and undo, full keyboard operation.
- 🟡 A deployed preview so a reviewer can run it.

*Stretch*

- 🟡 Offline-first: an IndexedDB outbox with idempotent replay and per-field last-write-wins
  conflict resolution keyed on `updatedAt` + `deviceId`.
- 🟡 Recurrence rules via `rrule`, expanded lazily over a 90-day horizon.
- 🟡 A hand-written windowing virtualiser for 10k tasks.
- 🔴 A time-travel debugger: a ring buffer of every action and resulting state with a scrubber.
- 🔴 `tsc --noEmit` in CI plus `eslint-plugin-typed-linting` and a type-coverage gate.
- ⚫ Property tests generating whole task graphs, not just action sequences.

**Architecture**

React + TypeScript, chosen because the reducer/selector split tests cleanly and the story is about
types rather than a framework.

- `src/domain/task.ts` — types only. No imports, no runtime logic beyond constructors.
- `src/domain/reducer.ts` — the pure reducer.
- `src/domain/selectors.ts` — memoised derived data: filter → sort → search.
- `src/domain/invariants.ts` — `assertInvariants(state)` used in dev mode and in tests.
- `src/data/repository.ts` / `localRepo.ts` / `indexedDbRepo.ts` — the persistence interface and
  two implementations.
- `src/state/AppContext.tsx` — provider wiring `useReducer` plus the undo log.
- `src/components/{TaskList,TaskRow,TaskEditor,FilterBar,SearchInput,ShortcutOverlay,UndoToast}.tsx`
- `src/test/` — co-located; no network to mock, so no `msw`.

Data model:

```ts
type TaskStatus = 'active' | 'completed' | 'archived';
type Priority = 'low' | 'normal' | 'high';

interface BaseTask {
  readonly id: TaskId;          // branded: string & { readonly __brand: 'TaskId' }
  readonly createdAt: number;   // epoch ms, injected
  readonly updatedAt: number;
  readonly revision: number;    // bumped per mutation, for optimistic concurrency
}
interface ActiveTask    extends BaseTask { status: 'active'; title: string; priority: Priority;
                                          dueAt: number | null; tags: readonly string[]; notes: string }
interface CompletedTask extends ActiveTask { status: 'completed'; completedAt: number }
interface ArchivedTask  extends BaseTask  { status: 'archived'; title: string; archivedAt: number;
                                          archivedFrom: 'completed' | 'active' }
type Task = ActiveTask | CompletedTask | ArchivedTask;

interface AppState {
  readonly tasks: readonly Task[];
  readonly filter: Filter;
  readonly query: string;
  readonly selection: readonly TaskId[];
  readonly undoStack: readonly UndoEntry[];
  readonly schemaVersion: number;
}

type Action =
  | { type: 'task/created';   payload: ActiveTask }
  | { type: 'task/completed'; payload: { id: TaskId; at: number } }
  | { type: 'task/reopened';  payload: { id: TaskId; at: number } }
  | { type: 'task/archived';  payload: { id: TaskId; at: number } }
  | { type: 'task/edited';    payload: { id: TaskId; patch: EditablePatch; at: number } }
  | { type: 'task/deleted';   payload: { id: TaskId; removed: Task } }
  | { type: 'task/restored';  payload: Task }
  | { type: 'filter/changed'; payload: Partial<Filter> }
  | { type: 'query/changed';  payload: string }
  | { type: 'selection/toggled'; payload: TaskId };
```

The union's payoff: `task/completed` only type-checks when the task is not already completed,
enforced at the reducer boundary, and a `switch` that misses a variant becomes a compile error via
`assertNever`.

Request paths (local-first, so these are read paths):

1. **Boot**: `getItem('tasks:v3')` → `JSON.parse` inside `try` → `migrate(raw, 3)` → reducer init
   → render. Parse or migration failure falls back to `[]` with a non-blocking banner, never a
   blank screen.
2. **Write**: dispatch → reducer → a `useEffect` on the tasks slice debounced 250ms →
   `repository.save`. Without the debounce, keystroke-rate edits serialise forty writes a second.
3. **Undo**: pop the last `UndoEntry` (the inverse action plus any removed task) and dispatch it.
   Memory is O(actions), not O(state size).
4. **Read model**: `selectVisibleTasks(state)` memoised on `(tasks, filter, query)` so selection
   changes do not re-run filtering.

**The hard parts**

1. **Making illegal states unrepresentable.** Discriminated union plus narrowing at the reducer
   boundary: each case asserts the current status, and the switch ends with
   `default: return assertNever(action)` where `assertNever` takes `never` and returns `never`.
   Add `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch` and `noImplicitReturns`. Adding a status field becomes a compile
   error everywhere it must be handled.
2. **A test suite that catches regressions rather than inflating a number.** Generate the reducer
   transition table over every `(status, action)` pair and assert the resulting status, the
   `revision`, and that untouched tasks are reference-equal — which catches accidental copies.
   Then `fast-check` properties: purity (`reduce(s, a)` twice deep-equals and never mutates a
   deep-frozen `s`), no loss (every id present before is present after, modulo explicit deletes),
   and undo fidelity (`undo(apply(s, a))` deep-equals `s`). Property tests find the bug you did not
   think of; that is the entire point.
3. **Migrations that never brick a returning user.** Store `{ version, data }` with pure
   `migrate1to2`, `migrate2to3`, reduced by a `migrate(raw)` dispatcher. Test each step with a
   fixture captured from the real old build, plus an e2e test that seeds v1 and asserts the user
   sees their tasks. Keep the original raw value until the new one is durably written, and wrap the
   write in `try` so a quota failure does not leave a half-migrated store.
4. **Undo without snapshots.** Each mutating action carries its inverse: `deleted` carries the
   removed `Task` so undo is a `restored` action; `edited` records the previous values of only the
   changed keys (diff the patch against current state); `completed` pairs with `reopened`. Cap at
   50 entries in a ring buffer. Have an answer ready for whether undo crosses filter changes — mine
   does, and it clears a filter that would hide the restored task, then announces it.
5. **Optimistic offline writes that converge.** A per-task `revision` checked on write; a pending
   queue in IndexedDB tagged with an `opId` so replay upserts by `opId` rather than appending; a
   conflict policy of last-write-wins *per field* with a recorded conflict log surfaced in a debug
   panel; and `online`/`offline` listeners to drain the queue. The detail that earns credit:
   per-field LWW, so a title edit on one device does not clobber a tag edit on another.

**Milestones**

| # | Task | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| M1 | Types and invariants: union, branded `TaskId`, `assertNever`, strict flags | 5h |
| M2 | Reducer complete: all actions, transitions, revision bumps | 6h |
| M3 | Property tests: purity, no-loss, undo fidelity, 1000 sequences | 5h |
| M4 | Persistence and migrations: repository interface, v1→v2→v3, failure fallback | 5h |
| M5 | UI: list, row, editor, filter, search, memoised selectors | 8h |
| M6 | Keyboard and a11y: shortcuts, focus management, live regions, listbox semantics | 5h |
| M7 | Undo/redo: inverse log, ring buffer, undo toast | 3h |
| M8 | E2E: Playwright config, three flows, CI on every push | 5h |
| M9 | Polish and deploy: error banner, empty states, perf, deploy | 4h |
| S | Stretch: IndexedDB outbox, time-travel debugger, virtualisation, recurrence | 8h |

~46h core, ~8h stretch.

**Evaluation rubric**

| Dimension | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TypeScript discipline | `any` everywhere | types in one file | discriminated unions, branded ids, `assertNever` | strict + `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, zero escapes, coverage gate |
| Domain modelling | booleans for status | optionals everywhere | union makes illegal states unrepresentable | plus invariants asserted in dev and tests |
| Reducer & state | scattered `setState` | one mutating reducer | pure reducer, injected time, memoised selectors | plus an action log enabling time travel |
| Tests | happy path only | some unit | unit + integration + property + e2e | properties that would have caught a real bug; coverage explained |
| Persistence | single blob | load and save | versioned schema, migrations, failure fallback | idempotent offline outbox with a conflict log |
| UX & a11y | mouse only | labels only | full keyboard, live regions, focus management | discoverable shortcut system, undo that respects the view |

**What an interviewer probes**

- "Why a union and not booleans?" Expect: illegal combinations become unrepresentable.
- "Show me a bug your property test found." Have a real answer; if you have never run them, say so
  and describe what you would assert.
- "How would you test undo?" Expect: inverse actions, not snapshots, plus a fidelity property.
- "What happens when the schema changes?" Expect: versioned payload, per-version pure migrations,
  fixtures from real old payloads.
- "How would this scale to 100k tasks?" Expect: virtualisation, and honest naming of what breaks
  first (recomputation per keystroke in search, then DOM count).

**Follow-on extension**

A real HTTP backend behind the same repository interface (`HttpRepo`) with optimistic UI and
rollback; request deduplication and a retry queue; an outbox with idempotency keys; sanitised error
reporting via an error boundary; OpenTelemetry spans around repository calls; a feature flag so the
time-travel debugger loads only when enabled; and a migration documented as reversible or explicitly
irreversible.
