**CAP, stated precisely so you do not say the meme.** During a network partition, a system must choose between remaining **available** (serving requests, possibly with stale data) and remaining **consistent** (all reads see the most recent write, refusing to serve otherwise). You cannot have all three simultaneously, and the choice only exists *during a partition*. Partition tolerance is not optional in a distributed system, so the real choice is C vs A. Also worth volunteering: PACELC extends it — if there is no partition, trade off availability vs latency (EL) instead.

**Consistency models, weak to strong.**

| Model | Guarantee | Where you see it |
|---|---|---|
| Eventual | All replicas converge eventually; reads may be stale | Default for caches, read replicas, DynamoDB, many NoSQL stores |
| Read-your-writes | You always see your own writes | Requires sticky routing or a causal token |
| Monotonic reads | Never see older data than you already read | Cheap-ish to implement |
| Monotonic writes | Writes are seen in order | Reasonable default target |
| Sequential | All processes see writes in the same order | Single-leader replication with a total order |
| Causal | Causally related writes are ordered, concurrent ones are not | Session guarantees |
| Linearizable | Every operation appears to take effect instantaneously between its invoke and response; preserves real time | Strongest single-object model; expensive |
| Strict serializability | Linearizable *and* serializable across objects | Costliest; hard to reason about, easy to test with Jepsen-style tools |

**The practical consistency choices.**

| Requirement | Choice |
|---|---|
| Money, inventory count, seat booking | Strong within the partition of authority; single writer; serializable or explicit locking |
| Likes, view counts, followers | Eventual; commutative/idempotent updates |
| Feeds | Eventual, with fan-out-on-write vs fan-out-on-read decided by write:read ratio and staleness tolerance |
| Sessions | Strong enough for read-your-writes; usually a single region or a sticky session |
| Catalog browse | Eventual with TTL-based invalidation |

**Strategies to buy consistency where you need it.** Synchronous replication (stronger, slower, still not linearizable without a consensus protocol). Consensus (Raft/Paxos) for single-leader linearizable writes. Leader-based routing with a lease. Read-your-writes via a version/timestamp carried by the client. Quorums (`R + W > N`) for overlap, plus `N`, `W`, `R` chosen deliberately. Version vectors or hybrid logical clocks for multi-region causal ordering. CRDTs for commutative merges (counters, sets, registers). Eventual consistency with a read-repair pass.

**Saga pattern.** Multi-participant operation as a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action. Compensating actions are not rollbacks (you cannot un-send an email) — design them as semantic opposites, and handle the unrecoverable cases explicitly (a compensating action itself fails). Choreography (event-driven, no orchestrator) versus orchestration (a central coordinator) — orchestration is easier to debug; choreography avoids the central bottleneck and the "god service".

**Outbox pattern.** Write the business change and an event record in the *same* database transaction; a relay reads the outbox and publishes to the broker, then marks it sent. Guarantees at-least-once with no lost events and no dual-write problem. Consume idempotently. Same shape for the *inbox* side (dedupe by event id).

**Idempotency, complete.**

| Aspect | Guidance |
|---|---|
| Definition | Repeating the request has the same effect as performing it once |
| Where to implement | Server-side, always; client-side retries only help if the server is idempotent |
| Idempotency key | Client-generated UUID sent in `Idempotency-Key` header, unique per logical operation |
| Storage | Store `{key, request hash, status code, response body}` with a TTL equal to your retry window |
| Atomicity | Insert the key with a unique constraint inside the same transaction as the effect; a duplicate insert means "already done, replay the stored response" |
| Same key, different body | Reject with `409` |
| Key scope | Per authenticated principal and per endpoint |
| HTTP mapping | `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent by definition; `POST` needs a key; `GET` must never mutate |
| TTL choice | Long enough to cover client retries and network partitions (24 h is common) |
| Distinguish from dedupe | Dedupe is by business identity; idempotency is by request identity |

**Retry safety rules.** Retry only idempotent operations. Exponential backoff with full jitter. Cap attempts and total elapsed time. Propagate a deadline/timeout budget through every hop. Never retry a non-idempotent operation without a key. Retry on `429`, `502`, `503`, `504`, and on network errors — never on `4xx` validation failures.

**Eventual-consistency UX, if asked.** Design the interface to tolerate staleness: show "updated N minutes ago", never present a conflicting write as a hard failure, prefer a read-your-own-writes path, and make the merge outcome predictable (CRDT or last-write-wins with a visible timestamp).

### K.2.14 Linux commands for debugging

🟢 Beginner · **Must-know** — you will be asked "how would you debug a slow server?"

**The reflex ladder for "the server is slow".**

| Step | Command | Reading it |
|---|---|---|
| Load average | `uptime`, `top` | >1 per core means saturated; Linux load also counts uninterruptible I/O |
| CPU by process | `top`, `htop`, `pidstat 1 5` | Is it my process or the kernel? |
| CPU by thread | `top -H -p <pid>`, `ps -L -p <pid>` | Java/JVM and async runtimes need thread-level view |
| Memory | `free -h`, `ps aux --sort=-%mem`, `pmap -p <pid>` | RSS vs virtual; swap usage; is it OOM-leaning? |
| I/O | `iostat -x 1`, `iotop`, `vmstat 1` | `%util` and `await` high = storage bound; `vmstat` `si`/`so` = swapping |
| Network | `ss -tunap`, `netstat -anp`, `ss -s` | Thousands in `SYN-RECV`/`TIME_WAIT` = connection churn |
| Disk usage | `df -h`, `du -sh /*`, `lsof | grep deleted` | Full disk is a top-three incident cause |
| Inodes | `df -i` | "No space left" with free space = inode exhaustion |
| Open files | `lsof -p <pid>`, `ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l` | File-descriptor leak |
| Kernel OOM kills | `dmesg -T | grep -i oom`, `journalctl -k` | Exit 137 explained |
| System calls | `strace -p <pid> -c`, `ltrace` | Is it blocked on I/O or spinning? |
| Process tree | `pstree -ap <pid>` | Zombie and orphan detection |

**Essential file and text tools.**

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Find a file | `find . -name '*.log' -mmin -60 -size +100M` |
| Fast content search | `rg -n 'pattern' -g '*.ts'` (ripgrep) |
| Follow a log | `tail -f`, `less +F` |
| Filter logs | `less +/ERROR` then `&pattern`, or `rg` |
| Count and aggregate | `awk '{print $1}' access.log \| sort \| uniq -c \| sort -rn \| head` |
| HTTP response timing | `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{time_namelookup} %{time_connect} %{time_starttransfer} %{time_total}\n' <url>` |
| DNS | `dig +short`, `dig +trace`, `nslookup`, `host` |
| Connectivity | `ping`, `traceroute`, `mtr`, `nc -zv host 443`, `curl -v` |
| TLS inspection | `openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host` |
| JSON in a terminal | `jq '.data[0]'`, `jq -r '.items[] | .id'` |
| Line endings / encoding | `file`, `dos2unix`, `iconv` |
| Binary encoding | `xxd`, `base64`, `od -c` |
| Permissions | `ls -l`, `namei -l /path/to/file`, `stat file` |
| Who owns it | `lsof -i :8080`, `ss -tunap \| grep 8080` |
| Env of a process | `cat /proc/<pid>/environ \| tr '\0' '\n'` |
| Start a command's stat | `/usr/bin/time -v <cmd>` |

**Signal vocabulary.**

| Signal | Number | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `SIGHUP` | 1 | Terminal closed; reload config |
| `SIGINT` | 2 | Ctrl-C; graceful shutdown request |
| `SIGQUIT` | 3 | Ctrl-\; produces a core dump |
| `SIGKILL` | 9 | Cannot be caught; the container was killed |
| `SIGTERM` | 15 | Graceful shutdown; your app must handle it |
| `SIGSTOP` | 19 | Pause |

**Process states.** `R` running, `S` interruptible sleep (normal), `D` uninterruptible I/O (a storage problem — this is what drives load average), `Z` zombie (needs a reap; a PID-1 that does not reap creates a leak), `T` stopped. A high `D`-state count is a disk-latency incident, not a CPU incident.

**Signal-handling rules that get asked.** PID 1 in a container does not get default signal actions, so your app must trap `SIGTERM` explicitly or Kubernetes will `SIGKILL` after the grace period. On shutdown: stop accepting new work, finish or hand off in-flight requests, flush logs, close database connections, then exit. Grace period must exceed your longest request or your drain budget.

**Production-safe reflexes.** `less` before `cat`. `head`/`tail` before `cat` on a 2 GB log. `du` before `rm`. `pgrep`/`pkill -f` with the full pattern, and check the PID list before killing. Copy a log off the box before rotating it. Never `kill -9` a process holding unflushed state unless you have to. `lsof` before you delete a file that is still open (deletion does not free space until the last descriptor closes).

### K.2.15 React rendering and hooks rules

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** — asked in nearly every frontend round.

**The mental model.** React re-runs a component function to produce a tree of React elements; React then diffs that against the previous tree and commits minimal host mutations. "Re-render" is a function call, not a DOM operation. A state update in a component re-renders that component and, unless memoized or stopped with a stable value, its children too.

**The hooks rules, with the reasons.**

| Rule | Reason |
|---|---|
| Only call hooks at the top level | Hooks use a linked-list ordering; a conditional call corrupts it |
| Only call hooks from React functions | Same linked list; the dispatcher is per-render |
| Names start with `use` | The lint rule enforces the above; it also documents intent |
| Custom hooks share logic, not state | Each call to a custom hook creates independent state |
| Effects run after commit, not during render | Reading/writing during render breaks concurrent rendering |

**Effect rules.**

| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Effects synchronize with something *outside* React | Subscriptions, network, timers, browser APIs, imperative DOM |
| Do not derive state in an effect | Compute during render or with `useMemo` instead |
| Every effect that subscribes/starts must clean up | Return a teardown function |
| Dependencies must be exhaustive | Otherwise stale closures; use a functional update or a ref to avoid the dependency instead |
| Avoid `useEffect` for event handlers | Those belong in render |
| Avoid `useEffect` for props→state sync | Do the mapping during render |
| `useEffect` cannot return anything but a function or undefined | Returning a value is an error |
| Two effects writing the same state | They can overwrite each other; fix with a single reducer |

**Common bug catalogue — know the fix for each.**

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| "Maximum update depth exceeded" | Effect sets state that re-triggers the effect, usually with an unstable dependency (new object/array each render) | Stabilize the dependency, remove the effect, or use a functional update |
| Stale closure in a timer | Effect/handler captured old props | Include deps, or hold the latest value in a ref |
| Effect runs twice | `StrictMode` in dev, or a remount from a changing `key` | Expected in dev; fix `key` stability |
| Child re-renders despite `React.memo` | A prop is a new object/array/function each render | Memoize the child prop with `useMemo`/`useCallback`, or pass primitives |
| Infinite fetch loop | Fetch in effect → set state → effect reruns | Fetch on mount with a stable key, or move to a data library / server component |
| State updates on an unmounted component warning | Async completion after unmount | Abort with `AbortController` and guard in cleanup |
| List animation broken | Keyed by index | Key by a stable identity |
| Form loses focus on every keystroke | Input value bound to state that resets, or component remounting from an unstable key | Stable key, keep the value in the parent or a ref if it is uncontrolled |
| Expensive list with per-item subscription | Subscription in each row | Subscribe once at the list level, or use `useSyncExternalStore` per row |
| Context update re-renders everything | One big context | Split state and dispatch contexts; memoize the provider value; or use a selector library |
| Debounce not cleared | Missing cleanup | Return `clearTimeout` from the effect |

**Performance measurement order.** React DevTools Profiler (why did it render, how long did it commit) → is the cost render or commit → are there long tasks → is the problem layout thrash or paint → only then reach for `memo`/`useMemo`/`useCallback`. Add memoization with evidence; unnecessary memoization is a net cost.

**The actual memoization rules.** `useMemo` for expensive computation or for a value used as a dependency or a `React.memo` prop. `useCallback` for a prop or a dependency — do not use it for a function you do not pass anywhere. `React.memo` for components whose props are shallow-stable. `useDeferredValue` for a value that may lag behind input (search results). `useTransition` for a non-urgent state update. `useId` for accessible generated ids. `useSyncExternalStore` for a subscription to an external store with correct tearing behaviour.

**`useReducer` vs `useState`.** Many interdependent fields or a multi-step UI → one reducer with explicit actions. Reducers are pure, so they are trivially testable and debuggable, and transition actions cannot half-apply.

**Server components and streaming.** Server components run once on the server, cannot use state or effects, and ship less JavaScript. The client boundary is where interactivity begins, and every boundary costs you a bundle. Use streaming with a `Suspense` boundary for slow regions, so TTFB is not blocked by the slowest query.

### K.2.16 Node event loop ordering

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** — asked specifically at Node-heavy companies.

**Phases of one loop turn.**

| Phase | What runs | Watch out |
|---|---|---|
| Timers | `setTimeout`, `setInterval` callbacks whose threshold elapsed | Minimum granularity ~1 ms; starvation of the loop delays all |
| Pending callbacks | Deferred, e.g. some TCP errors | Rarely relevant |
| Poll | Retrieve new I/O events; execute I/O callbacks | **If no timer and fewer than 4 pending, the poll blocks** — this is why the loop can idle |
| Check | `setImmediate` callbacks | Runs after poll |
| Close callbacks | `socket.on('close')`, `server.close` | |
| process.nextTick queue | Drained **between every phase and after each callback** | Microtask priority: highest |
| Promise microtasks | Drained after the nextTick queue | |

**Ordering rules to state.**

1. `process.nextTick` callbacks run before promise microtasks.
2. Promise microtasks drain completely before the next macrotask.
3. `setImmediate` fires before `setTimeout(fn, 0)` **when called from inside the main module**, and the reverse **when called from inside an I/O callback**. This is not a bug; it is the poll phase's blocking behaviour.
4. A `setImmediate` scheduled from a `setTimeout(0)` runs after that timer.
5. Microtask starvation blocks the loop entirely — a recursive `nextTick` will freeze the process.

**Worked order example.**

```js
console.log('1: sync');
setTimeout(() => console.log('5: timeout'));
setImmediate(() => console.log('6: immediate'));
process.nextTick(() => console.log('3: nextTick'));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('4: promise'));
console.log('2: sync end');
```
Output: `1, 2, 3, 4, [5 or 6 in either order, stable within a run], 6/5`. The `nextTick` and promise lines are guaranteed; the timer/immediate pair is not — state that explicitly, it is the classic answer.

**Blocking the loop.** `JSON.parse` on a huge payload, `fs.readFileSync`/`existsSync`, synchronous crypto (`pbkdf2Sync`), a `while` loop, regex backtracking, sorting a million items, template rendering of a giant string, or 10,000 `await`s of already-resolved promises. Symptom: p99 latency spikes while CPU sits at one core. Fixes: worker threads, a worker pool (`piscina`, `node:worker_threads`), chunk the work, or move it to another process.

**libuv thread pool.** Four threads by default (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`) serving `fs`, `dns.lookup`, `crypto`, and `zlib`. Raise it for CPU-heavy work; note `fs` itself is mostly async via the thread pool. `dns.resolve*` is genuinely async (c-ares); `dns.lookup` uses the thread pool (getaddrinfo).

**Async error handling.** `async`/`await` inside a `try/catch` works for awaited rejections. Unawaited promise rejections crash Node 15+ by default — always `await` or attach a `.catch`. `setTimeout` and most callback APIs cannot reject, so wrap them. Use `events.once`/`promisify` for callback APIs. Handle `uncaughtException` only to log and exit gracefully, never to keep running in a possibly corrupt state.

**Graceful shutdown pattern.**

```js
process.on('SIGTERM', async () => {
  server.close();                    // stop accepting new connections
  await drainInFlightRequests();      // finish what is in flight
  await closePoolAndDb();
  process.exit(0);
});
process.on('SIGINT', shutdown);
```
Set a hard deadline and exit non-zero if the drain exceeds the orchestrator's grace period.

**Timeouts and cancellation.** Always pass an `AbortSignal` for network calls so a shutdown or a request abort actually cancels work. Set timeouts on every outbound call — a hung upstream is a production incident. Prefer a request-scoped deadline propagated to downstream calls.

**Async control-flow tools.** `Promise.all` (fail fast, all resolved), `Promise.allSettled` (need every outcome), `Promise.any` (first success), `Promise.race` (first settlement — often the right way to implement a timeout). `AbortController`/`AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` for cancellation. Streams (`Readable.from`, `pipeline` which propagates errors and cleans up) for large payloads. `async` iterators plus `for await` for sequential backpressure. `p-limit` for concurrency caps.

**Connection pooling and throughput.** Keep-alive agents and connection reuse. `http.globalAgent.maxSockets` tuned. `pg.Pool` sizing — total connections across instances must stay under the Postgres limit. Node's per-process model means horizontal scaling is process/thread based, and a single-threaded runtime is a hard ceiling per core.

### K.2.17 Auth flows: OAuth and PKCE, and JWT validation

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** — security interviews ask exactly here.

**OAuth 2.0 roles.** Resource owner (the user), client (your app), authorization server, resource server (your API). Authorization code flow is the only flow you should recommend for anything with a confidential server or any mobile/SPA client.

**Authorization Code flow (backend).**

```
1. GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=...&redirect_uri=...
        &scope=openid profile email&state=<random>&code_challenge=...&code_challenge_method=S256
2. User authenticates and consents at the auth server
3. Auth server 302s to your redirect_uri with ?code=...&state=...
4. Backend verifies state, then POSTs to /token with
        grant_type=authorization_code, code, redirect_uri,
        client_id, client_secret, code_verifier
5. Auth server returns { access_token, refresh_token (optional), id_token, expires_in, token_type }
6. Backend calls the userinfo or /me endpoint to fetch claims
```

**PKCE, spelled out.** The verifier is a high-entropy random string (43–128 chars). The challenge is `BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier))` with `code_challenge_method=S256` (`plain` is legacy and only for the odd client that cannot do SHA-256). The token request must send the same verifier. This binds the authorization code to the client that requested it, so an intercepted code is useless. Required for public clients: SPAs, mobile apps, CLIs.

**`state`.** A random, unguessable value stored in the user's session and compared on callback. It is CSRF protection for the callback. Multiple concurrent logins need multiple states (a list keyed by nonce), and they must be single-use.

**Which token to use where.**

| Token | Audience | Sent to | Verified by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access token | The resource server (your API) | `Authorization: Bearer` to the API | The API, against the issuer's public key |
| ID token | Your client, for "who is the user" | Nowhere; read claims locally after validating | The client, then only trust claims |
| Refresh token | The authorization server | The token endpoint only | The auth server |

**`nonce`.** A random value in the auth request, echoed in the ID token, and required to be validated — it prevents replay of an ID token and ID-token substitution attacks. Not a replacement for `state`.

**JWT validation — the complete checklist.**

| Check | Meaning | Failure mode it prevents |
|---|---|---|
| Algorithm allow-list | Only the expected algorithms; reject `none` and any asymmetric↔symmetric confusion | Algorithm confusion attacks |
| Signature | Verify with the issuer's key, from the JWKS endpoint, cached | Forged tokens |
| `iss` | Exactly your authorization server | Tokens from another tenant/issuer |
| `aud` | Your API identifier is in the audience | Token replay against a different service |
| `exp` | Not expired; allow a small clock skew (≤60 s) | Reuse of stale tokens |
| `nbf` | Not before now, if present | Clock skew |
| `iat` | Sane; not absurdly old | Very long-lived leaked tokens |
| `jti` | For access tokens: not in a revocation list, if your threat model needs it | Logout does not revoke |
| Scope/roles | Required scope present for this endpoint | Privilege escalation |
| Subject | `sub` matches the resource owner you expect | Confused-deputy / tenant crossover |

**Where to validate.** At the API gateway *and* in the service. A gateway-only check means a bug in any other ingress path bypasses auth entirely. Validate the signature once per key version, cache the parsed claims per request (not per call site), and never trust a claim that came from a client-provided header without validating its provenance.

**Access token storage (the browser question).**

| Option | Storage | Risk | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cookie, `HttpOnly`+`Secure`+`SameSite=Lax` | Browser cookie, not readable by JS | CSRF (mitigated by `SameSite` + a CSRF token for state-changing requests) | Best for a server-rendered or hybrid app |
| Cookie with access token, `httpOnly` false | Readable by JS | XSS steals it | Avoid |
| Token in `localStorage` | Readable by JS | XSS steals it, and it survives forever | Avoid for long-lived tokens |
| BFF pattern | Browser holds only an `HttpOnly` session cookie; a backend-for-frontend holds the tokens | Best isolation | Best practice for high-value apps |

Add `Clear-Site-Data` on logout. Rotate the refresh token on every use and detect reuse (a reused refresh token implies theft — revoke the whole family). Keep access tokens short-lived (5–15 min for high-value apps, up to an hour otherwise). Support revocation and `token_type_hint`; hash tokens at rest.

**JWT pitfalls to name.** Payload is base64, not encrypted — never put secrets in a JWT. `kid` lets you rotate keys; publish a new key and keep the old one for the overlap window. `jwks_uri` caching with a TTL; refetch on an unknown `kid`. Do not put large arrays in a header or payload (size limits at the gateway). Revocation via a denylist re-introduces state, which is why short lifetimes exist. Asymmetric (RS256/ES256/EdDSA) beats HS256 for multi-service setups, because only the auth server can mint.

**Session vs JWT.**

| Dimension | Server session | JWT |
|---|---|---|
| Revocation | Immediate | Hard (denylist or short lifetime) |
| State on the server | Required | Not required |
| Horizontal scaling | Needs a shared store | Stateless |
| Token size | Tiny cookie | 1–3 KB in the header |
| Failure mode | Store down = nobody logs in | Still validates if keys are cached |
| Best for | Traditional web apps | Service-to-service, mobile, third-party APIs |

**Passkeys and WebAuthn — one line.** Public-key, phishing-resistant, no shared secret; the server stores a public key and challenges are signed by the device. The forward-looking answer to password phishing.

### K.2.18 LLM integration: streaming, tools, RAG parameters

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** — increasingly asked at AI-heavy companies.

**Request anatomy.** An LLM call is: a system prompt, a conversation history, the current user message, optional retrieved context, an optional tool/function schema, and sampling parameters. You are building a deterministic system around a non-deterministic component.

**Sampling parameters.**

| Parameter | Range | What it does | Practical note |
|---|---|---|---|
| `temperature` | 0–2 | Scales the logit distribution before sampling | 0 for classification/extraction/code; ~0.7 for creative writing. Many APIs accept 0 as greedy decoding |
| `top_p` (nucleus) | 0–1 | Sample from the smallest set of tokens whose probability mass is `top_p` | Interacts with temperature; tune one, not both |
| `top_k` | integer | Limit candidates to the k highest-probability tokens | Available on some providers |
| `max_tokens` / `max_output_tokens` | integer | Cap output length | Budget it; this is your main cost and latency control |
| `stop` | strings | Stop sequences | Useful for classification output formats |
| `seed` | integer | Deterministic sampling where supported | Not a guarantee across model versions |
| `presence_penalty` / `frequency_penalty` | -2–2 | Discourage repetition | Useful for long generations |
| `n` | integer | Number of candidates | Multiply cost linearly; usually you want 1 |
| `logprobs` / `top_logprobs` | int | Per-token probabilities | For confidence scoring, reranking, debugging |
| `response_format` / structured outputs | schema | Constrains the output to a schema | Strongly preferred over asking for JSON in prose |

**Prompting that holds up.**

| Technique | Effect |
|---|---|
| Few-shot examples | Biggest cheap win for format and tone consistency |
| Explicit output schema + a validation step | Turns a formatting failure into a retryable error rather than a crash |
| Delimit user content (and instruct the model to ignore instructions inside it) | Reduces prompt injection from retrieved/user content |
| Chain-of-thought for reasoning tasks | Only for tasks that need it; it costs latency and tokens |
| ReAct-style "thought then tool" scaffolding | Better than unstructured CoT for tool use |
| Break a task into ordered steps in the prompt | Reduces omitted-step errors |
| Ask for citations/quotes from the provided context | Measurably reduces hallucination |
| Precompute what does not need the model | Token/prompt caching for static prefixes |

**Structured output.** Ask for a schema, get a schema-constrained response, then *validate with a real validator* (the schema guarantees shape, not that the values are correct). On validation failure: retry once with the error appended, then fail gracefully.

**Streaming.**

| Aspect | Guidance |
|---|---|
| Transport | Server-sent events for one-way; WebSockets only if you need bidirectional |
| Why | Time-to-first-token is the perceived-latency metric; a stream shows output in ~300 ms even if total time is unchanged |
| Chunk format | Provider-specific deltas; normalize to your own event shape |
| Backpressure | Flush per chunk; buffer if the consumer cannot keep up |
| Cancellation | Client disconnect must abort the upstream call — otherwise you pay for tokens nobody sees |
| Frontend | Stream into a buffer, append deltas; handle out-of-order and partial-JSON (a structured output streamed is only parseable at the end) |
| Observability | Log TTFT, total latency, token counts, finish reason (`stop`/`length`/`tool_call`/`content_filter`) |

**Tool calling (function calling).**

| Step | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| 1 | You send tool definitions: name, description, and a JSON Schema for parameters |
| 2 | The model replies with a tool call: tool name plus a JSON arguments object (finish reason `tool_calls`) |
| 3 | **You** execute it, with your own auth, validation, and timeouts |
| 4 | Append the tool result to the conversation and call again |
| 5 | Repeat until the model returns a final answer with no tool calls |
| Pitfalls | Validate every argument server-side; the model is an untrusted input source. Enforce timeouts. Cap the loop iterations. Tool descriptions are prompt surface — be precise. Return errors as data the model can reason about, not exceptions. Never let the model call anything with credentials it obtained. Parallel tool calls in one turn are supported by most providers — handle them concurrently |

**RAG: the pipeline and its parameters.**

| Stage | Options and parameters |
|---|---|
| Chunking | Fixed size (256–1024 tokens typical), recursive character split, sentence/paragraph, semantic chunking, late chunking. Chunks: ~200–800 tokens, 10–20% overlap. Too small loses context; too large dilutes the embedding |
| Embeddings | Model choice, dimension (384/768/1536/3072), `normalize` embeddings, batch size, document vs query prefixes (`search_document` vs `search_query` for asymmetric models) |
| Index | Flat (exact, `inner_product`/`cosine`) for < ~100k vectors; HNSW (fast, tunable) for more. HNSW tuning: `M` (graph degree, 16–64), `ef_construction` (100–500, quality vs build time), and `ef_search`/`k` at query time (higher = better recall, slower) |
| Search | Top-k (3–10 typically), hybrid (dense + BM25, fused with RRF), metadata filters, query rewriting or expansion, multi-query for recall |
| Reranking | Cross-encoder rerank of the top-k (better precision, adds ~100–300 ms). Often the single biggest quality win |
| Prompt assembly | Context window budget; put the most relevant chunks near the query; number and cite sources; do not truncate silently |
| Generation | Temperature 0 for grounded QA; instruct "answer only from the context, and say you do not know" |
| Answer construction | Return citations mapped to chunk ids so the UI can show them |
| Evaluation | Retrieval: recall@k, MRR, nDCG. Generation: faithfulness/groundedness, answer relevance, citation precision. Golden dataset of ~50–200 questions; measure regressions on every change |

**Cost and latency arithmetic.** Input tokens ≈ `chars/4` for English. Cost = `input_tokens × in_price + output_tokens × out_price`. Cache static prefixes (system prompt, few-shot examples, tool schemas) to cut input cost dramatically. Latency ≈ `prefill (proportional to input) + decode (proportional to output × per-token time)`, so long outputs are disproportionately expensive in time — cap `max_tokens`, stream, and prefer structured brevity.

**The rest of the system, which is what senior candidates add.** A retrieval service with its own index lifecycle; document parsing and chunk refresh; per-tenant isolation and access filtering *before* retrieval (filter by ACL in the query, not after generation); caching keyed on the normalized query plus corpus version; a fallback to no-context; a circuit breaker around the model provider; streaming with abort; cost and quality dashboards; an eval harness in CI; and a clear answer that the deterministic parts (permissions, business rules, arithmetic) belong in code, not in the prompt.

---

## K.3 Common Mistakes by Phase

Each phase has a signature way of failing. The mistake is rarely ignorance — it is a specific, predictable error of judgement. Format is: **the mistake → why it costs the interview → the fix.**

### K.3.1 PHASE 1 — Interview Preparation Foundations

| Mistake | Why it costs the interview | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Reading the roadmap, never speaking | You build recognition, not recall. In the interview you must produce the answer under pressure | Every topic gets a 30-second spoken answer. Out loud, standing up, timed |
| Practising only easy problems | You train under conditions you will never face, then the real interview feels impossible | Cap your practice at 20% easy. If you solve it in under 10 minutes, it was too easy |
| Resuming the "grind everything" habit | Coverage feels like progress; the interview tests depth on ~15 topics | Pick your top 15 topics per role. Extra breadth is worth almost nothing |
| No mock interviews until the end | The failure mode you never trained is *being watched while thinking* | Three mocks in week one, then weekly. Diagnostics first |
| Treating a mock as a verdict | You catastrophize after one bad hour, or ignore one good hour | Trend rule: average the last three mocks. Never react to one |
| Not fixing the diagnostic | You repeat the same mistake for four weeks because mocks "feel bad" | Every mock produces exactly one written fix and one next drill |
| Ignoring logistics | Wrong link, no scratchpad, no water, wrong version of the repo — you burn 10 minutes and your confidence | Run the pre-flight checklist (K.1.1) every time, including mocks |
| Cramming the last 3 days | Sleep-deprived recall is much worse than rested recall; familiarity feels like mastery | Taper (K.5.4). Review notes, do not learn new material |
| Only practising "how" and never "why" | You can recite a pattern but cannot adapt it when the prompt is unusual | For every algorithm, write the trade-off sentence |
| Not writing down your three weakest skills | You spend revision time on what you are already good at | Rank by (mock score × role weight) and fix the top three |

### K.3.2 PHASE 2 — Absolute Foundations

| Mistake | Why it costs the interview | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Memorizing definitions without mechanisms | "A hash table is O(1)" is useless when asked *why* | Learn the mechanism: bucketing, collision resolution, load factor, resize |
| Omitting amortized analysis | Dynamic array append and hash map insert are not strictly O(1) | Say "amortized O(1)" and explain doubling |
| Ignoring the CPU/memory/I-O division | Every scaling answer depends on knowing what you are bottlenecking on | One paragraph: CPU-bound scales by cores, I/O-bound by concurrency |
| Confusing process and thread | Classic tell for a junior; undermines every concurrency answer | PID is the container, threads share the address space and the heap |
| Blurring TCP and UDP | Cannot explain the handshake, head-of-line blocking, or congestion control | Be able to contrast them in a table, out loud |
| Skipping recursion→iteration conversion | Asked constantly for linked lists, trees, and stack-overflow avoidance | Do 10 conversions; know the manual-stack pattern |
| Not knowing how a hash can be broken | "Hash is O(1)" with no collision story invites "what if the adversary picks the keys" | Explain chaining, open addressing, and tree-mode escalation |
| Confusing big-O with wall-clock | You pick a theoretically better structure that is slower in practice | Compare constants and cache behaviour; state the crossover point |
| Answering "it depends" with nothing | It reads as an evasion, not a nuance | Follow every "it depends" with the actual decision criteria |
| No understanding of encoding and compression | Unicode bugs and "why is the payload smaller" both need it | Know UTF-8 byte length vs character length, base64 overhead (+33%) |

### K.3.3 PHASE 3 — Frontend Foundations (HTML, CSS, JS, TS, browser internals)

| Mistake | Why it costs the interview | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Treating the DOM as a tree it is not | Cannot explain reflow, repaint, or why layout thrashing is slow | Model: DOM tree → CSSOM → render tree → layout → paint → composite |
| Not knowing the event loop's ordering guarantees | The single most common frontend technical question | Be able to run the `console.log` ordering example live and explain why |
| Confusing `==` and `===` as a style rule | The real answer is coercion and `Object.is` edge cases | Teach coercion: `null == undefined`, `NaN === NaN` is false, `-0` |
| Ignoring scope and closures | Callback-in-loop bugs, stale closures, and `var` vs `let` all trace here | `let` per-iteration binding; closures capture the binding, not the value |
| Assuming `Promise.all` is always right | It fails fast and gives partial visibility; the correct answer is situational | `all` vs `allSettled` vs `any` vs `race` with a use case each |
| `async` function treated as synchronous | `await` inside a loop; unhandled rejections crashing the process | `await` in a loop for dependent work; `Promise.all` for independent work |
| Not knowing how a bundler works | Cannot debug a duplicate-library or a missing-export problem | Module resolution, tree shaking *reality*, code splitting, source maps |
| Under-estimating CSS specificity wars | Live-coding a component degrades into `!important` escalation | Learn the cascade: origin, importance, layer, specificity, order |
| Accessibility treated as a checkbox | `<div onClick>` fails in front-end screens | Semantic elements, focus order, keyboard paths, ARIA only where native fails |
| No performance vocabulary | "It feels slow" is not an answer | Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP, CLS, plus TTFB and long tasks |
| Muddling `type` and `interface` | Signals shallow TypeScript knowledge | `interface` for extension/augmentation, `type` for unions and mapped types |
| Not knowing what TypeScript erases | `as`, enums, and param properties confuse the runtime story | Types vanish; enums and namespaces emit code; param properties emit assignments |

### K.3.4 PHASE 4 — Frontend Frameworks (React, Next.js, state, FE architecture)

| Mistake | Why it costs the interview | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Misunderstanding "re-render" | The core mental model is wrong, so every performance answer is wrong | Component function re-runs → diff → commit. React elements are immutable descriptions |
| Effects used as a state machine | Effect→setState→effect loops are the #1 React bug | Derive during render; sync only external systems; one reducer for UI state |
| Blind `useEffect` deps | Stale closures, or a rule-of-hooks-looking eslint-disable | Exhaustive deps, or deliberately restructure to remove the dependency |
| `useCallback`/`useMemo` everywhere | Adds cost and hides the real bottleneck; reads as cargo cult | Memoize with a measured reason: expensive compute, memo-child prop, or dependency |
| Keying lists by index | Breaks state, focus, and animation on reorder | Stable entity id |
| One giant context | Every consumer re-renders on any change | Split contexts, memoize the value, or use a selector store |
| Not knowing when to use a state machine | Multi-step forms produce a tangle of booleans | Explicit states and transitions; it is testable by construction |
| Data fetching mishmash | Ad-hoc fetch + effects + loading flags + race conditions | A query library with cache keys, or a server-side fetch. Cancel stale requests |
| Vague frontend system design | "Use Redux" is not a design | Start from the requirements: SEO, data volume, interaction model, bundle budget, team size |
| Not knowing rendering strategies | Cannot reason about SSR/SSG/ISR/streaming trade-offs | When data is known at build → SSG; per-request → SSR; interval → ISR; client-only → CSR; slow → streaming |
| Ignoring error/loading/empty states | The interviewer notices the gap immediately | Define all four states in the design, including the partial-failure case |
| Skipping accessibility in the design | Front-end systems design rounds score it | Keyboard path, focus management, semantic landmarks in the plan |

### K.3.5 PHASE 5 — Backend Foundations (Node, Express, Nest, REST, GraphQL, queues)

| Mistake | Why it costs the interview | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Blocking the event loop | The most damaging Node-specific error you can make live | No sync fs/crypto, no heavy CPU on the main thread, no `forEach` with async inside |
| No transactions around a multi-write mutation | Half-written state is the reliability story of your whole system | One transaction; or a saga with compensating actions if it crosses services |
| N+1 queries | Both a performance and a design-review smell | `JOIN`, `DataLoader`/batching, or a denormalized read model |
| Returning 200 for everything | Shows no HTTP semantics | 201/204/400/401/403/404/409/422/429, chosen deliberately |
| No idempotency on a retried POST | Double charges, double emails | `Idempotency-Key` + a unique-constraint-backed store of the response |
| Hand-rolled auth (roll your own JWT/session) | Security review fail | Use vetted libraries; understand the flow well enough to audit them |
| Framework-first, no design | Code without boundaries; tests impossible | Route → controller → service → repository, with validation at the edge |
| No structured logging or request IDs | You cannot debug your own system in a real incident | JSON logs with a correlation id, propagated to every downstream call |
| Fire-and-forget async work | Silent loss; no backpressure | A queue with retries, a DLQ, idempotent consumers, and lag alerting |
| Misusing GraphQL | N+1, no depth limiting, no query cost limits, no persisted queries | Batching, depth/complexity limits, timeouts, persisted queries |
| Ignoring timeouts and cancellation | One slow dependency becomes an outage | Timeout + `AbortSignal` on every outbound call; propagate deadlines |
| No graceful shutdown | In-flight requests die; connection pools leak | Trap `SIGTERM`, drain, close, exit |

### K.3.6 PHASE 6 — Database Systems (SQL, indexing, NoSQL, caching, modeling)

| Mistake | Why it costs the interview | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `SELECT *` everywhere | Network, plan, and coupling costs | Project only what you need; it is also a schema-change safety tool |
| Missing indexes on filter/sort/join columns | The database becomes the bottleneck in every design round | Index the equality prefix, then range, then `ORDER BY` columns |
| N+1 without noticing | The single most common performance question | `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` every query you write in practice; batch with `IN` or a join |
| Misunderstanding joins and NULLs | Silent wrong answers in analytics queries | `NOT IN` with NULLs, `LEFT JOIN` predicates in `WHERE`, three-valued logic |
| No transaction isolation reasoning | Lost updates and phantom reads in real code | Name the anomaly you are preventing; choose the weakest sufficient level; or use optimistic locking |
| Treating Redis as a database | Data loss, eviction surprises, single point of failure | Cache-aside, TTL + jitter, warm on first miss, monitor the hit rate |
| Cache stampede | One popular key expiring takes down the origin | Single-flight / distributed lock around repopulation; randomized TTL |
| Not modelling for the access pattern | A "correct" schema that cannot serve the hot query | Start the model from the two or three hottest queries |
| Assuming NoSQL avoids schema | Uncontrolled data drift and impossible migrations | Schema discipline regardless of engine; migrations for documents too |
| Missing foreign key indexes | Cascades and joins table-scan | Index every FK; the DB does not do it for you (Postgres) |
| Believing denormalization is free | Two write paths that drift | Denormalize deliberately: one writer, a reconciliation job, and a defined repair path |
| No plan for growth | Single-node ceiling accepted until the incident | Know your partition key, your read-replica strategy, and your hot-partition risk |

### K.3.7 PHASE 7 — Networking and Security

| Mistake | Why it costs the interview | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Calling 401 "unauthorized" | Everyone does it; nobody has thought | 401 = unauthenticated, 403 = authenticated but not allowed |
| "CORS is a security feature" | Shows a category error | CORS is a browser policy; authz must be enforced server-side |
| Not explaining the TLS handshake | Asked in most networking rounds | DNS → TCP → TLS (1–2 RTT) → request → response, with certificate verification named |
| Confusing stateless and stateful | "Sessions are in cookies" is not an explanation | Where the state lives, how it is validated, how it scales |
| Storing tokens in `localStorage` | XSS turns into account takeover | `HttpOnly` cookie or a BFF holding the tokens |
| Trusting client input | The interviewer's favourite trap | Validate at the edge, constrain at the DB, parameterize queries, least privilege |
| Missing idempotency | Double side effects on retry | Key + atomic store; see K.2.13 |
| No threat model when asked about security | Generic "use HTTPS and bcrypt" | Name assets, trust boundaries, the top three threats, and a control for each |
| "Encrypt everything" | No threat model, no key management | TLS in transit, encryption at rest with managed keys, least privilege, audit trail |
| Confusing cookie flags | `Secure` and `SameSite` are the ones people miss | `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/` as the default reflex |
| Ignoring DNS, or blaming it | A classic "5 minutes of downtime" war story | Cache TTLs, health-checked registries, and multiple resolvers |
| Cannot debug with `curl -v` and `dig` | Looks helpless in a debugging question | Be fluent with `-w` timing, `-v`, `--resolve`, and `dig +trace` |

### K.3.8 PHASE 8 — DevOps and Cloud

| Mistake | Why it costs the interview | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `latest` tags everywhere | Unreproducible builds; a surprise upgrade at 2 a.m. | Pin versions, ideally by digest, and rebuild deliberately |
| Running as root in a container | Immediate security-review finding | `USER` in the Dockerfile; read-only root fs where possible |
| Secrets in build args or `ENV` | Baked into image layers and visible in `docker inspect` | Runtime secret injection from a secret manager |
| No health checks | Orchestrators route traffic to a dead process | `HEALTHCHECK` or probes, with thresholds matched to real start-up time |
| Missing resource requests/limits | Scheduling is a guess; noisy neighbours; OOM kills | Requests from observed usage, limits with headroom; watch CPU throttling |
| Layer ordering in a Dockerfile | Every code change reinstalls every dependency | Copy manifests first, install, then copy source |
| `npm start` as the entrypoint | No signal forwarding; no graceful shutdown | Exec the binary directly: `CMD ["node","dist/main.js"]` |
| Zero-downtime deploys assumed | Rolling update that breaks in-flight requests or breaks on schema change | Backward-compatible migrations, expand-then-contract, readiness gates |
| No rollback plan | "We would roll forward and hope" | Immutable artifacts + a rehearsed rollback; know your MTTR |
| Treating IaC as a formality | Drift between reality and code, discovered during an incident | Remote state, plan-as-review, drift detection in the pipeline |
| Not knowing the debugging ladder | Frozen in the first minute of a live scenario | `get → describe → logs --previous → events → exec → ephemeral debug container` |
| Blaming the orchestrator | Reads as immaturity | Name the actual failure mode: OOM, probe, image pull, resource starvation, config |

### K.3.9 PHASE 9 — Testing Strategies

| Mistake | Why it costs the interview | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Snapshot tests as the default | Fail on irrelevant changes, pass on wrong behaviour | Assert behaviour and outcomes; use snapshots only for genuinely stable shapes |
| Mocking the unit under test | Tests that can never fail | Mock at the boundary; never mock what you are testing |
| "We mock the database" called an integration test | Misrepresentation interviewers catch instantly | Real DB in a container for anything transactional |
| Chasing 100% coverage | Vanity metric; tests the getters | Cover boundaries and error paths; use coverage to find untested risk, not as a goal |
| Sleeping instead of awaiting | Flaky suite nobody trusts | Await a condition, poll with a deadline, use deterministic fixtures |
| No test for the incident | The same bug ships twice | Add a regression test in the same PR that fixes a production bug |
| Shared mutable state | Order dependence; CI failures unrelated to code change | Fresh DB transaction per test, or a fresh container per suite |
| Non-deterministic time and randomness | Heisenbugs | Inject a clock; seed the RNG; never assert on real randomness |
| No load or performance test | "It will scale" with no evidence | A k6 script asserting p95/p99 at 2× expected peak, run pre-release |
| Cannot name what you do not test | You have not thought about risk | State the gaps: third-party internals, browser quirks, chaos paths |
| E2E-only suites | Slow, flaky, unmaintainable | Pyramid: many fast unit/component tests, few integration, very few E2E |

### K.3.10 PHASE 10 — Coding Challenges, CS Fundamentals, DSA

| Mistake | Why it costs the interview | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Coding before clarifying | You build the wrong thing and lose the whole round | 3–5 questions: inputs, outputs, scale, edge cases, constraints |
| Silence while thinking | The interviewer cannot help you and starts doubting you | Narrate intent: "now I need the window, so two-pointer" |
| No testing before declaring done | Self-caught bugs are the only ones that are cheap | Trace 2 cases manually, then run the code, then test an edge case |
| LeetCode-only pattern matching | You cannot adapt when the pattern does not fit | Derive the structure from the access pattern; practice non-LeetCode variants |
| Guessing complexity without stating it | Confidently wrong is worse than unsure | State time and space per operation, then the total |
| Over-engineering the solution | Beautiful, slow, and unfinished | Ship the simplest correct solution, then optimize if time remains |
| Running out of time | Zero credit for an unfinished design | Time-box: 5 min clarify, 15 min solve, 5 min test, 5 min complexity + edge cases |
| Panicking after getting stuck | The recovery is worth points | Restate the problem, try the brute force, then look for the structure; say what you are trying |
| Not deriving the naive solution first | Loses the structural insight and looks magic | Always state brute force + its complexity, then improve |
| No communication during optimization | A perfect answer scores as a partial one | Explain each change and its effect on complexity |
| Ignoring the "why this company" and shipping generic answers | Every answer reads as rehearsed from a template | Anchor each answer to something specific about the role or the product |
| Practising only questions you have seen | Memorized solutions score well at home, badly in the room | At least half your practice must be unseen problems |

### K.3.11 PHASE 11 — Architecture Patterns and Low-Level Design

| Mistake | Why it costs the interview | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Name-dropping patterns without applying them | "We used microservices" is not a design | State the problem, the constraint, the pattern, and what it costs |
| Repository/Service layers for a 3-endpoint app | Ceremony that hides the real logic | Add a layer when the boundary pays for itself |
| Dependency inversion as a diagram | Nobody asks for SOLID by acronym | Explain testability and substitutability as the goal |
| Event bus used as a dumping ground | Untraceable coupling; cycles | Typed events, a documented contract, and an owner per event |
| Microservices without boundaries | Distributed monolith; network latency tax | Boundaries by domain and team ownership; a monolith is often the right answer |
| Caching everything, invalidating nothing | The #1 source of stale-data bugs | Cache-aside, TTL, explicit invalidation, and a documented staleness contract |
| Ignoring failure modes | "What if the payment service is down?" ruins it | Timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, queues, compensations |
| Not knowing when *not* to scale out | Over-engineered interview answer | Single node with a cache is often the correct first step |
| Failing to discuss the data model | The data model is the design | Entities, access patterns, growth, and the primary key strategy |
| Skipping deployment and rollback | Half the design is missing | How it ships, how it is monitored, how it is rolled back |
| No cost discussion | Not required, but it signals senior judgement | Name the expensive parts; "we'd use a managed service here" |
| No alternative considered | One solution, no trade-off reasoning | Always give 2 options and the criteria that decide between them |

### K.3.12 PHASE 12 — System Design

| Mistake | Why it costs the interview | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| No numbers in the first 5 minutes | Looks like you are guessing scale | DAU → QPS → storage → bandwidth, with the arithmetic spoken aloud |
| Jumping to a diagram before requirements | The diagram will be wrong | Functional requirements, then non-functional, then the numbers, then the design |
| Designing for 10M when asked about 1,000 | Signals you are not listening | Anchor to the given scale, then say what breaks at 100× |
| Solving a different problem than asked | Fatal and common with URL shorteners and chat | Clarify: who writes, who reads, what must be fast, what must be durable |
| Database as the only component | Misses the caching and read-scaling story | Include cache, queue, blob store, and search where the data shape demands it |
| No failure discussion | Interviewers wait for it | What happens when the cache dies, the queue lags, a region goes dark, a shard is hot |
| No data-partitioning strategy | The scaling answer is incomplete | Shard key, rebalancing, hot-partition risk, cross-shard query handling |
| Ignoring the read/write path asymmetry | Misses feeds, timelines, and analytics entirely | "Writes are 1% of traffic" → denormalize and fan out on read |
| No observability or alerting | Half of production readiness | SLIs, dashboards, alerts on symptoms, runbooks |
| Choosing consistency everywhere | Unbuildable, and it shows | Consistency per operation, with an explicit boundary and a staleness contract |
| Talking for 50 minutes | You get cut off before the follow-ups | Hit your checkpoints: requirements by 5 min, data model by 15, deep dive by 30 |
| Not thinking out loud | Silent whiteboard work reads as flailing | Label boxes, arrows, and data flow; say what you are deciding and why |

### K.3.13 PHASE 13 — AI-Era Full Stack Skills

| Mistake | Why it costs the interview | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Calling a model API and calling it done | No evaluation, no cost control, no failure handling | Prompt → structured output → validation → eval → monitor |
| No structured output | Fragile parsing of prose that "usually" works | Schema-constrained output plus a real validator plus one retry |
| Trusting model output | Hallucination, injection, invalid tool arguments | Treat the model as an untrusted input source; validate everything |
| Prompt injection ignored | The single most discussed security issue in LLM apps | Isolate retrieved/user content, delimit it, never give the model credentials, validate tool args |
| Permissions checked after generation | Leaks data through the answer | Filter by ACL *before* retrieval; never post-filter a generation |
| RAG with a bad chunking strategy | Retrieval recall is capped no matter how good the model is | Chunk 200–800 tokens with overlap; semantic or late chunking for structure |
| No reranking | Low precision drowns the answer in distractors | Cross-encoder rerank of the top-k; usually the biggest single quality win |
| Cost blindness | A single feature can be a monthly bill | Track cost per request and per feature; cap `max_tokens`; cache prefixes |
| No latency strategy | A 20 s answer is unusable even if correct | Stream, show TTFT, parallelize retrieval and tools, prefer smaller models for routing |
| No eval set | You cannot tell whether a change helped | 50–200 golden questions; recall@k + faithfulness; run in CI |
| Forgetting the boring 80% | The interview is still mostly systems | Queueing, rate limits, auth, audit logs, cost dashboards, fallbacks |
| Claiming AI replaces a component | Signals trend-following rather than judgement | Say which parts are deterministic code, which are model calls, and why |

### K.3.14 PHASE 14 — Behavioral and Engineering Culture

| Mistake | Why it costs the interview | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| "We did X" — no personal ownership | The interviewer cannot tell what you did | "I decided X over Y because Z" |
| Rambling for 4 minutes | Loses the room, loses the point | One sentence situation, the decision, the quantified result, one learning |
| No metrics | Unverifiable; reads as small | Before/after numbers: latency, incidents, revenue, adoption, effort saved |
| No failure story | Implies you have never failed, or you hide | Have a real failure with a real postmortem and a systemic fix |
| Blaming other people | Fatal in a culture screen | Own your part, name the system failure that allowed it |
| Inconsistent story | Cross-round contradictions are noticed | One canonical set of eight stories (K.1.4) |
| Only recency, no depth | Surface-level | Follow any project with: why built, alternatives rejected, what broke, what you would change |
| Generic reverse questions | Wastes the last 10 minutes, which is where offers are decided | Ask about on-call, incident history, and what they decided *not* to build |
| Arguing about tech in a culture round | Almost always reads badly | Disagree with evidence, then commit; say "I would want to try that" |
| Over-sharing (health, family, burnout) | Unprofessional context | Keep it professional; if you must mention constraints, keep it to one neutral sentence |
| Rehearsed-sounding answers | Everyone knows a rehearsed answer | Prepare structure and content, not a script; let the specifics be real |
| No questions about the team | Signals you do not care about the work | Ask two technical and one process question |

### K.3.15 PHASE 15 — Job Search, Offers, and Career

| Mistake | Why it costs the interview | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Applying to 100 roles a week | Neither side is serious; your prep does not improve | 8–15 well-targeted applications a week, with a tailored resume |
| One generic resume for every role | Rejected before a human reads it | Mirror the job description's language and lead with relevant evidence |
| Weak follow-up after the interview | The decision is often made in the 48-hour window | Thank-you note within 24 hours, referencing a specific detail, plus one useful addition |
| Asking about salary too early | Anchors low or disqualifies you | Ask about range after you have an offer and understand scope |
| Comparing offers on base alone | You lose 30–50% of the value | Total comp, vesting, equity (ask the strike price and refresh schedule), location factor, on-call, severance |
| No negotiation at all | The most expensive mistake in the whole process | Always negotiate; the offer is not final. Anchor above the midpoint, cite your leverage |
| Asking for an offer without leverage | Weak position | Interview well, have a second pipeline, and get the offer in writing before negotiating |
| Ignoring the take-home | A cheap way to fail after passing the loop | Treat it as a real feature: tests, README, error handling, deploy notes |
| Burning bridges after an offer | The industry is small; people talk | Decline professionally and keep the recruiter relationship |
| Neglecting the pipeline during a long process | Offers dry up while you wait | Keep interviewing until the offer is signed |
| No post-mortem after each loop | You repeat the same failure 20 times | Score every round with K.1, write one fix, repeat |

### K.3.16 Cross-cutting mistakes (all phases)

| Mistake | Why it costs the interview | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Hedging everything | "I think maybe sort is O(n log n)" | Know it, state it, name the assumption it depends on |
| Answering only what was asked | Misses the follow-up you were set up for | Answer, then add the one thing they did not ask but should |
| Silence as a strategy | Reads as not knowing | Think aloud; "let me check the edge case" is a legitimate phrase |
| Arguing with the interviewer | Never helps | Concede quickly, then show the alternative in a follow-up |
| Jargon without substance | Detected instantly | Plain language first, term second |
| No numbers anywhere | Unfalsifiable claims | Every scale, latency, and impact claim gets a number or an explicit "I'd measure" |
| Guessing confidently | A single wrong fact undermines the right ones | "I'm not certain; my understanding is X, and I'd verify with Y" |
| Coding without ever testing | Only self-caught bugs are cheap | Trace, run, test an edge case, then talk about the edges |
| Ignoring the follow-up questions | They are the real evaluation | Answer in depth; if it is a system design, re-open the design |
| Treating the interviewer as an adversary | The collaboration is the evaluation | Treat it as a pair designing together; ask them to challenge you |
| Not asking what a good answer looks like | You optimize for the wrong thing | Early on: "what would you consider a strong answer here?" |
| Perfectionism in revision | Reading without output | Every hour of revision ends with something spoken or written |
| Burning out the week before | Fatigue is visible in every signal | Sleep is a study technique, not a cost |
| No feedback loop | You repeat mistakes indefinitely | Score, record, fix one thing, re-score |

---

## K.4 Rapid-Fire Bank (150 questions with one-to-two-sentence answers)

Answer these aloud in under 30 seconds each. If you cannot, that is your revision list.

**Foundations (1–20)**

1. **O(1) vs O(log n)?** Array indexing is a fixed number of machine operations; a tree descent is one step per level, so it scales with height.
2. **Why is binary search O(log n)?** Each comparison halves the search space, so n → n/2 → n/4, reaching 1 in log₂(n) steps.
3. **Amortized O(1) means?** The total cost over n operations is O(n) even though individual operations can be O(n) — like doubling a dynamic array.
4. **Hash table worst case?** O(n) when all keys collide into one bucket; mitigated by chaining, tree-mode escalation, or randomization.
5. **Stack vs heap allocation?** Stack is LIFO, contiguous, automatic lifetime, fast; heap is dynamic, manual/GC lifetime, slower to access.
6. **Process vs thread?** A process has its own address space; threads share the heap and file descriptors but have their own stack and registers.
7. **Race condition?** Two threads access shared state without synchronization, producing a result dependent on interleaving.
8. **Deadlock requires?** Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait — break any one.
9. **Mutex vs semaphore?** A mutex is binary ownership of one resource; a semaphore is a counter allowing N concurrent holders.
10. **TCP vs UDP?** TCP gives ordered, reliable, congestion-controlled delivery; UDP is connectionless with no guarantees but no head-of-line blocking.
11. **Why head-of-line blocking in TCP?** Ordered delivery means a lost segment stalls all later data on the connection.
12. **Three-way handshake?** SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — it synchronizes sequence numbers and establishes the connection state.
13. **Time complexity of Python `+` on strings?** O(n) per append because strings are immutable, so a loop is O(n²); use `join`.
14. **Bit vs byte?** A bit is one binary digit; a byte is 8 bits. Storage is measured in bytes; speed in bits per second.
15. **Encoding vs encryption?** Encoding is a reversible representation change (base64, UTF-8); encryption requires a key to reverse.
16. **Big-O vs Big-Theta?** Big-O is an upper bound; Big-Theta is a tight bound; Big-Omega is a lower bound.
17. **Recursion → iteration?** Use an explicit stack (or queue for BFS), which removes call-stack overhead and the depth limit.
18. **Why is quicksort average O(n log n) and worst O(n²)?** Partitioning is linear per level; worst-case pivots give n levels instead of log n.
19. **In-place means?** Constant extra space beyond the input — not necessarily O(1) time.
20. **What is a hash collision and how do you handle it?** Two keys map to the same bucket; handle by chaining (separate lists), open addressing with probing, or rehashing.

**Frontend (21–45)**

21. **Event bubbling vs capturing?** Events propagate target → ancestors (bubble) or window → target (capture); the bubble phase is the default handler phase.
22. **What causes a reflow?** Changing geometry-affecting properties (width, content, position) forces layout recomputation; read-then-write in a loop causes thrashing.
23. **Event loop in the browser?** macrotask queue (timers, I/O) → render opportunity → microtask queue (promises) drains completely first.
24. **`==` vs `===`?** Loose uses type coercion (`null == undefined` is true); strict compares type and value.
25. **`null` vs `undefined`?** `undefined` means "no value assigned"; `null` means explicitly "no object/value".
26. **Closure?** A function plus the lexical environment it captured when created.
27. **`var` in a loop with `setTimeout`?** All callbacks see the final value because `var` is function-scoped; `let` creates a per-iteration binding.
28. **Hoisting?** Declarations are moved to the top of their scope; `var` becomes `undefined`, function declarations are initialized, `let`/`const` are in the temporal dead zone.
29. **`Promise.all` vs `allSettled`?** `all` resolves when all resolve and rejects on the first rejection; `allSettled` always waits and reports every outcome.
30. **What is a microtask?** A job in the microtask queue — promise callbacks and `queueMicrotask` — drained before the next macrotask.
31. **`useEffect` dependency array?** The values from render that the effect closes over; omitting one gives a stale closure, so include all or restructure.
32. **Why key lists by id?** React uses keys to decide which nodes to reuse; index keys misidentify nodes after reorder and corrupt state, focus, and animation.
33. **What does React re-render mean?** The component function re-runs and returns a new element tree; React then diffs and commits minimal DOM changes.
34. **`useMemo` vs `useCallback`?** `useMemo` caches a computed value; `useCallback` caches a function identity. Both are for referential stability or expensive work.
35. **What is a render-prop vs hook?** A render-prop is a function child receiving data; a hook is a function called inside a component that may use state and effects.
36. **Context vs Redux/Zustand?** Context propagates a value; a store adds subscriptions, selectors, and devtools, so only the components that read a slice re-render.
37. **LCP, INP, CLS?** Largest Contentful Paint (load), Interaction to Next Paint (responsiveness), Cumulative Layout Shift (visual stability).
38. **How do you fix a large CLS?** Reserve space for async content (`width`/`height` or `aspect-ratio`), avoid inserting content above existing content, use skeletons with exact dimensions.
39. **What is code splitting?** Dynamic `import()` creates separate chunks loaded on demand, reducing initial bundle and enabling per-route loading.
40. **SSR vs CSR vs SSG vs ISR?** Server-render per request, render in the browser, generate at build time, or regenerate at build time and on an interval — pick by data freshness and SEO needs.
41. **Hydration mismatch?** Server and client rendered different markup; caused by `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, locale, or browser-only APIs in render — fix by deferring to an effect or using `suppressHydrationWarning` sparingly.
42. **Semantic HTML matters because?** It gives free accessibility (focus, roles, semantics for assistive tech) and correct default behaviour.
43. **`box-sizing: border-box`?** Padding and border are included in the declared width, which makes layout arithmetic predictable.
44. **Specificity order?** Inline style > ID > class/attribute/pseudo-class > element/pseudo-element; `!important` overrides normal declarations.
45. **What causes a memory leak in SPAs?** Unremoved event listeners, timers, subscriptions, detached DOM references, or unbounded caches — every one is a cleanup responsibility.

**Backend / API (46–70)**

46. **Idempotency key?** A client-generated unique token so a retried request has the same effect as the original; stored atomically with the response.
47. **How do you store an idempotency key?** Unique index in the same transaction as the effect, with the request hash and cached response, plus a TTL.
48. **422 vs 400?** 400 for malformed/invalid syntax; 422 for well-formed but semantically invalid (business-rule validation failures).
49. **Pagination: offset vs cursor?** Offset is simple but breaks under concurrent inserts and is O(offset); cursor is stable and O(log n) but cannot jump to page N.
50. **N+1 query and fix?** A query per result row; fix with a join, an `IN` batch, or DataLoader-style batching.
51. **Idempotency vs deduplication?** Idempotency is per logical request; dedupe is per business entity (do not double-count this order).
52. **Rate limit algorithm?** Token bucket allows bursts up to the bucket size with controlled refill; sliding window avoids the boundary burst of fixed windows; leaky bucket smooths output.
53. **Circuit breaker?** After N failures it opens and short-circuits calls; it half-opens periodically to probe recovery — prevents cascading failure.
54. **Retry with jitter?** Exponential backoff spreads retries so clients do not resynchronize and hammer a recovering dependency.
55. **Optimistic vs pessimistic locking?** Optimistic checks a version at commit and fails fast (good for low contention); pessimistic holds a lock/row lock upfront.
56. **What is a write-ahead log?** An append-only durability log written before the data pages, making crash recovery replay-based rather than page-write-based.
57. **How do you handle a slow dependency?** Timeout + circuit breaker + degrade to a cached or partial response, plus an SLO and an alert on the degradation.
58. **REST idempotency?** `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE` are idempotent by definition; `POST` is not, so it needs an idempotency key.
59. **Message queue vs pub/sub?** A queue delivers to one consumer per message (competing consumers); pub/sub delivers to all subscribers but is lossy if they are offline.
60. **At-least-once vs exactly-once delivery?** At-least-once may duplicate (consumers must be idempotent); exactly-once is effectively only achievable end-to-end with idempotency and transactions.
61. **Dead letter queue?** Where permanently failing messages go, for inspection and replay — otherwise a poison message blocks the queue.
62. **What is a saga?** A distributed transaction as a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions.
63. **What is an outbox pattern?** Writing the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the data change, then relaying it — solves the dual-write problem.
64. **GraphQL N+1 fix?** DataLoader batching per request — the resolver returns a promise that a per-request batcher resolves in one query.
65. **GraphQL depth/complexity limiting?** Protects against nested and aliased-query abuse that would otherwise be a trivial DoS.
66. **Webhook signature verification?** HMAC over the raw body plus a timestamp, with a replay window and constant-time comparison.
67. **API versioning strategy?** Additive changes by default; major version in the path for breaking changes; `Sunset` header and a deprecation date.
68. **gRPC vs REST at scale?** Protobuf is smaller and HTTP/2 multiplexes, cutting latency; not worth it for browser clients or public APIs.
69. **What is a timeout budget?** A deadline propagated across the call chain so downstream calls fail before the upstream deadline, avoiding wasted work.
70. **How do you validate input at the edge?** Schema validation (Zod/Joi/JSON Schema) plus coercion, applied to params, query, headers, and body — before business logic.

**Database (71–95)**

71. **Composite index `(a, b)` — can I query on `b` alone?** Not efficiently; only the leading column is used, because the index is sorted by `a` first.
72. **Why does `WHERE DATE(created_at) = ...` not use the index?** The function on the column makes it non-sargable — index `created_at` and range a timestamp window instead.
73. **What is a composite index and how do you order its columns?** Equality columns first (most selective), then range, then sort columns; it also serves covering reads if columns are included.
74. **N+1 in SQL vs in code?** Same problem: one query per row in code; fix with joins or `IN` batching, and cache aggressively.
75. **`COUNT(*)` vs `COUNT(col)`?** The former counts rows, the latter skips NULLs — a common reporting bug.
76. **`DELETE` vs `TRUNCATE`?** `DELETE` is logged row by row and fires triggers; `TRUNCATE` is faster but resets identity and needs higher privileges.
77. **MVCC?** Multi-version concurrency control: readers see a consistent snapshot while writers create new row versions — the basis of Postgres's read consistency.
78. **What is a deadlock?** Two transactions hold conflicting locks and wait for each other; the DB detects it and aborts one.
79. **`NOT IN` with NULLs?** Returns zero rows if any subquery value is NULL — use `NOT EXISTS`.
80. **`LEFT JOIN` predicate in `WHERE`?** Converts it to an inner join, dropping unmatched rows — move the right-side predicate into `ON`.
81. **What is an index-only scan?** Reading entirely from the index — needs a covering index and a fresh visibility map; breaks under heavy updates.
82. **Sequential vs random I/O?** Sequential is much faster per byte; indexes are B-trees precisely to avoid it.
83. **Normalization vs denormalization?** Normalize for integrity and write correctness; denormalize for read performance, accepting a repair path.
84. **Connection pooling?** Reuse connections (bounded) — creation is expensive and unbounded connections exhaust the DB.
85. **Sharding strategies?** Hash (even spread, no range queries), range (range queries, hot partition risk), time (append-only, current period hot).
86. **How do you keep a hot partition from melting?** Split the partition key further, spread across shards with a salt or bucket, or move to a real data store.
87. **Read replicas?** Scale reads; they are stale (replication lag) — never read-after-write from a replica without a causal guard.
88. **`UNION` vs `UNION ALL`?** `UNION` dedupes and sorts; `UNION ALL` does neither — use it when duplicates are impossible for speed.
89. **Window function vs GROUP BY?** A window function does not collapse rows; it exposes per-row values alongside the aggregate.
90. **`ROW_NUMBER` vs `RANK`?** `ROW_NUMBER` never ties; `RANK` ties share a rank and gaps follow — matters for top-N logic.
91. **What is a partial index?** An index with a `WHERE` clause, so it is smaller and cheaper — ideal for a hot subset of a large table.
92. **When do you denormalize a counter?** Reads vastly exceed writes and exactness is not required — update asynchronously with an idempotent increment.
93. **What causes a slow query after adding an index?** Usually a write-amplified table, a stale plan, or a different access pattern; check with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`.
94. **What is a covering index?** An index containing every column the query needs, allowing an index-only scan.
95. **How do you safely add an index to a big table?** Build concurrently, then verify; never lock writes on a hot table.

**DevOps / infra (96–115)**

96. **Container vs VM?** Containers share the host kernel (fast, less isolation); VMs include a kernel (slower, stronger isolation).
97. **What is a multi-stage build?** Compiles in one stage and copies only the artifacts into a clean final stage, leaving build tools behind.
98. **Why order layers carefully?** Docker caches per layer; copying the source before installing dependencies invalidates the dependency layer on every change.
99. **What is a readiness vs liveness probe?** Readiness controls traffic routing; liveness controls restarts — never point liveness at a dependency.
100. **Why set resource limits?** Requests drive scheduling; limits prevent one pod from starving the node (CPU throttling, OOM).
101. **Rolling update vs blue/green?** Rolling keeps capacity lower and is slower to revert; blue/green is instant but doubles infrastructure.
102. **Why is a schema migration risky?** Incompatible code and schema coexist during a rolling deploy — use expand-then-contract.
103. **What does a graceful shutdown do?** Stop accepting new requests, finish in-flight work, close connections, exit — within the grace period.
104. **What is a CI gate?** A stage that blocks the pipeline (tests, lint, scan) — a failing gate must fail the pipeline.
105. **Immutable artifacts?** Build once, promote the same image through environments — the only way to know what actually shipped.
106. **What is Terraform state?** The mapping of real infrastructure to config — lock it remotely, back it up, and review plans as code.
107. **Config vs secret?** Config can live in a ConfigMap; secrets need a secret manager, rotation, and least-privilege access.
108. **What causes `ImagePullBackOff`?** Wrong tag, missing pull secret, registry auth, or a rate limit — check `describe pod` events.
109. **What causes `CrashLoopBackOff`?** The container starts and exits; read `logs --previous` — often a crash, a missing secret, or a failing probe.
110. **What is OOMKilled?** The container exceeded its memory limit (exit 137); raise the limit or reduce memory pressure.
111. **Horizontal vs vertical scaling?** Horizontal adds replicas (needs statelessness); vertical grows one instance (simple, has a ceiling).
112. **What is a liveness/readiness/startup probe?** Startup lets a slow app finish booting; liveness restarts a dead one; readiness gates traffic.
113. **Spot vs on-demand?** Spot is cheap but preemptible — right for batch and stateless workloads, wrong for singletons.
114. **What is a PDB?** A budget that keeps N replicas up during voluntary drains, so a node maintenance does not take out capacity.
115. **What is a base image concern you always mention?** Pinned version and digest, plus a scan, since `latest` is a moving target.

**Testing (116–125)**

116. **Unit vs integration?** Unit is fast and isolated; integration crosses a boundary (DB, HTTP) and proves the pieces work together.
117. **What is a contract test?** A test asserting two services agree on the message shape — the safety net for microservice changes.
118. **What does a fake vs a mock mean?** A fake is a working simplified implementation; a mock asserts on interactions rather than returning values.
119. **What is a snapshot test good for?** Stable serialized output (render trees, API responses) — not for asserting behaviour you care about.
120. **What is a test pyramid?** Many unit tests, fewer integration, very few E2E — fast feedback, lower flake.
121. **How do you test async code?** Await promises, use fake timers for time, poll with a deadline instead of sleeping.
122. **What is property-based testing?** Generate many inputs and assert invariants — finds edge cases you did not think of.
123. **Should you mock the DB in unit tests?** No if you are testing data access; use a real DB in a container for those tests.
124. **What is a regression test?** A test added for a fixed bug so it cannot return — required practice, not optional.
125. **What is a load test for?** Verifying latency and error rate under expected (and 2×) traffic — a claim about scalability needs evidence.

**System design (126–140)**

126. **Estimate QPS from DAU.** DAU × actions/day ÷ 86,400 = average; peak is typically 2–4× average.
